entries.427c613d7da75281e4c3e9af4a98b362886d3ffd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv90"/><title type="x-ms">Song of Solomon</title> <div sID="gen15174" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15175" type="x-p"/> All <hi type="italic">scripture,</hi> we are sure, <hi type="italic">is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable</hi> for the support and advancement of the interests of his kingdom among men, and it is never the less so for there being found in it some things <hi type="italic">dark and hard to be understood, which those that are unlearned and unstable wrest to their own destruction.</hi> In our belief both of the divine extraction and of the spiritual exposition of this book we are confirmed by the ancient, constant, and concurring testimony both of the church of the Jews, to whom were <hi type="italic">committed the oracles of God,</hi> and who never made any doubt of the authority of this book, and of the Christian church, which happily succeeds them in that trust and honour. I. It must be confessed, on the one hand, that if he who barely reads this book be asked, as the eunuch was <hi type="italic">Understandest thou what thou readest?</hi> he will have more reason than he had to say, <hi type="italic">How can I, except some man shall guide me?</hi> The books of scripture-history and prophecy are very much like one another, but this <hi type="italic">Song of Solomon's</hi> is very much unlike the songs of his father David; here is not the name of God in it; it is never quoted in the New Testament; we find not in it any expressions of natural religion or pious devotion, no, nor is it introduced by vision, or any of the marks of immediate revelation. It seems as hard as any part of scripture to be made a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life,</hi> nay, and to those who come to the reading of it with carnal minds and corrupt affections, it is in danger of being made a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> it is a flower out of which they extract poison; and therefore the Jewish doctors advised their young people not to read it till they were thirty years old, lest by the abuse of that which is most pure and sacred (<hi type="italic">horrendum dictu—horrible to say!</hi>) the flames of lust should be kindled with fire from heaven, which is intended for the altar only. But, II. It must be confessed, on the other hand, that with the help of the many faithful guides we have for the understanding of this book it appears to be a very bright and powerful ray of heavenly light, admirable fitted to excite pious and devout affections in holy souls, to draw out their desires towards God, to increase their delight in him, and improve their acquaintance and communion with him. It is an allegory, the letter of which kills those who rest in that and look no further, but the spirit of which gives life, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2 Cor. iii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.63">John vi. 63</reference>. It is a parable, which makes divine things more difficult to those who do not love them, but more plain and pleasant to those who do, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.14">Matt. xiii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.16">16</reference>. Experienced Christians here find a counterpart of their experiences, and to them it is intelligible, while <hi type="italic">those</hi> neither understand it nor relish it who have no part nor lot in the matter. It is a son, an <hi type="italic">Epithalamium,</hi> or nuptial song, wherein, by the expressions of love between a bridegroom and his bride, are set forth and illustrated the mutual affections that pass between God and a distinguished remnant of mankind. It is a pastoral; the bride and bridegroom, for the more lively representation of humility and innocence, are brought in as a shepherd and his shepherdess. Now, 1. This song might easily be taken in a spiritual sense by the Jewish church, for whose use it was first composed, and was so taken, as appears by the Chaldee-Paraphrase and the most ancient Jewish expositors. God betrothed the people of Israel to himself; he entered into covenant with them, and it was a marriage-covenant. He had given abundant proofs of his love to them, and required of them that they should love him with all their heart and soul. Idolatry was often spoken of as spiritual adultery, and doting upon idols, to prevent which this song was penned, representing the complacency which God took in Israel and which Israel ought to take in God, and encouraging them to continue faithful to him, though he might seem sometimes to withdraw and hide himself from them, and to wait for the further manifestation of himself in the promised Messiah. 2. It may more easily be taken in a spiritual sense by the Christian church, because the condescensions and communications of divine love appear more rich and free under the gospel than they did under the law, and the communion between heaven and earth more familiar. God sometimes spoke of himself as the husband of the Jewish church (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa. lxiv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.16">Hos. ii. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">19</reference>), and rejoiced in it as his bride, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.4-Isa.62.5">Isa. lxii. 4, 5</reference>. But more frequently is Christ represented as the bridegroom of his church (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Matt. xxv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">Rom. vii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2 Cor. xi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">Eph. v. 32</reference>), and the church as the bride, the Lamb's wife, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2 Rev.21.9">xxi. 2, 9</reference>. Pursuant to this metaphor Christ and the church in general, Christ and particular believers, are here discoursing with abundance of mutual esteem and endearment. The best key to this book is the <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">45th Psalm</reference>, which we find applied to Christ in the New Testament, and therefore this ought to be so too. It requires some pains to find out what may, probably, be the meaning of the Holy Spirit in the several parts of this book; as David's songs are many of them level to the capacity of the meanest, and there are shallows in them learned, and there are depths in it in which an elephant may swim. But, when the meaning is found out, it will be of admirable use to excite pious and devout affections in us; and the same truths which are plainly laid down in other scriptures when they are extracted out of this come to the soul with a more pleasing power. When we apply ourselves to the study of this book we must not only, with Moses and Joshua, <hi type="italic">put off our shoe from off our foot,</hi> and even forget that we have bodies, because <hi type="italic">the place where we stand is holy ground,</hi> but we must, with John, <hi type="italic">come up hither,</hi> must spread our wings, take a noble flight, and soar upwards, till by faith and holy love we <hi type="italic">enter into the holiest,</hi> for <hi type="italic">this is no other than the house of God and this is the gate of heaven.</hi> <div eID="gen15175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15176" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15177" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, after the title of the book (<reference osisRef="Song.1.1">ver. 1</reference>), we have Christ and his church, Christ and a believer, expressing their esteem for each other. I. The bride, the church, speaks to the bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2-Song.1.4">ver. 2-4</reference>), to the daughters of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5-Song.1.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>), and then to the bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Song.1.7">ver. 7</reference>. II. Christ, the bridegroom, speaks in answer to the complaints and requests of his spouse, <reference osisRef="Song.1.8-Song.1.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. III. The church expresses the great value she has for Christ, and the delights she takes in communion with him, <reference osisRef="Song.1.12-Song.1.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. IV. Christ commends the church's beauty, <reference osisRef="Song.1.15">ver. 15</reference>. V. The church returns the commendation, <reference osisRef="Song.1.16-Song.1.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. Where there is a fire of true love to Christ in the heart this will be of use to blow it up into a flame. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv90"/> <div eID="gen15177" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15176" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Title of the Book.</title> <div sID="gen15178" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The song of songs, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> Solomon's. <div eID="gen15178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15179" type="x-p"/> We have here the title of this book, showing, 1. The nature of it; it is a <hi type="italic">song,</hi> that it might the better answer the intention, which is to stir up the affections and to heat them, which poetry will be very instrumental to do. The subject is pleasing, and therefore fit to be treated of in a song, in singing which we may <hi type="italic">make melody with our hearts unto the Lord.</hi> It is evangelical; and gospel-times should be times of joy, for gospel-grace puts a <hi type="italic">new song</hi> into our mouths, <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Ps. xcviii. 1</reference>. 2. The dignity of it; it is <hi type="italic">the song of songs,</hi> a most excellent song, not only above any human composition, or above all other songs which Solomon penned, but even above any other of the scripture-songs, as having more of Christ in it. 3. The penman of it; it is Solomon's. It is not the song of fools, as many of the songs of love are, but the song of the wisest of men; nor can any man give a better proof of his wisdom than to celebrate the love of God to mankind and to excite his own love to God and that of others with it. Solomon's songs were a thousand and five (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1 Kings iv. 32</reference>); those that were of other subjects are lost, but this of seraphic love remains, and will to the end of time. Solomon, like his father, was addicted to poetry, and, which way soever a man's genius lies, he should endeavor to honour God and edify the church with it. One of Solomon's names was <hi type="italic">Jedidiah</hi>—<hi type="italic">beloved of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2 Sam. xii. 25</reference>); and none so fit to write of the Lord's love as he that had himself so great an interest in it; none of all the apostles wrote so much of love as he that was himself the beloved disciple and lay in Christ's bosom. Solomon, as a king, had great affairs to mind and manage, which took up much of his thoughts and time, yet he found heart and leisure for this and other religious exercises. Men of business ought to be devout men, and not to think that business will excuse them from that which is every man's great business—to keep up communion with God. It is not certain when Solomon penned this sacred song. Some think that he penned it after he recovered himself by the grace of God from his backslidings, as a further proof of his repentance, and as if by doing good to many with this song he would atone for the hurt he had perhaps done with loose, vain, amorous songs, when he <hi type="italic">loved many strange wives;</hi> now he turned his wit the right way. It is more probable that he penned it in the beginning of his time, while he kept close to God and kept up his communion with him; and perhaps he put this song, with his father's psalms, into the hands of the chief musician, for the service of the temple, not without a key to it, for the right understanding of it. Some think that it was penned upon occasion of his marriage with Pharaoh's daughter, but that is uncertain; the tower of Lebanon, which is mentioned in this book (<reference osisRef="Song.7.4">ch. vii. 4</reference>), was not built, as is supposed, till long after the marriage. We may reasonably think that when in the height of his prosperity he <hi type="italic">loved the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.3">1 Kings iii. 3</reference>) he thus <hi type="italic">served him with joyfulness and gladness of heart in the abundance of all things.</hi> It may be rendered, <hi type="italic">The song of songs, which is concerning Solomon,</hi> who as the son and successor of David, on whom the covenant of royalty was entailed, as the founder of the temple, and as one that excelled in wisdom and wealth, was a type of Christ, in whom are <hi type="italic">hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,</hi> and yet is a greater than Solomon; this is therefore a song concerning him. It is here fitly placed after <hi type="italic">Ecclesiastes;</hi> for when by the book we are thoroughly convinced of the vanity of the creature, and its insufficiency to satisfy us and make a happiness for us, we shall be quickened to seek for happiness in the love of Christ, and that true transcendent pleasure which is to be found only in communion with God through him. The voice in the wilderness, that was to prepare Christ's way, cried, <hi type="italic">All flesh is grass.</hi>
entries.16cdf97b0b4468fdf8c0e485ac79f31fa022a412: <div eID="gen15179" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than wine. <hi type="super">3</hi> Because of the savour of thy good ointments thy name <hi type="italic">is as</hi> ointment poured forth, therefore do the virgins love thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee. <hi type="super">5</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon. <hi type="super">6</hi> Look not upon me, because I <hi type="italic">am</hi> black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother's children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; <hi type="italic">but</hi> mine own vineyard have I not kept. <div eID="gen15180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15181" type="x-p"/> The spouse, in this dramatic poem, is here first introduced addressing herself to the bridegroom and then to the daughters of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen15181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15182" type="x-p"/> I. To the bridegroom, not giving him any name or title, but beginning abruptly: <hi type="italic">Let him kiss me;</hi> like Mary Magdalen to the supposed gardener (<reference osisRef="John.20.15">John xx. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">If thou have borne him hence,</hi> meaning Christ, but not naming him. The heart has been before taken up with the thoughts of him, and to this relative those thoughts were the antecedent, that good matter which the heart was inditing, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Ps. xlv. 1</reference>. Those that are full of Christ themselves are ready to think that others should be so too. Two things the spouse desires, and pleases herself with the thoughts of:— <div eID="gen15182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15183" type="x-p"/> 1. The bridegroom's friendship (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,</hi> that is, be reconciled to me, and let me know that he is so; let me have the token of his favour." Thus the Old-Testament church desired Christ's manifesting himself in the flesh, to be no longer under the law as a schoolmaster, under a dispensation of bondage and terror, but to receive the communications of divine grace in the gospel, in which God is reconciling the world unto himself, binding up and healing what by the law was torn and smitten; as the mother kisses the child that she has chidden. "Let him no longer send to me, but come himself, no longer speak by angels and prophets, but let me have the word of his own mouth, those <hi type="italic">gracious words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Luke iv. 22</reference>), which will be to me as the <hi type="italic">kisses of the mouth,</hi> sure tokens of reconciliation, as Esau's kissing Jacob was." All gospel duty is summed up in our kissing the Son (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Ps. ii. 12</reference>); so all gospel-grace is summed up in his kissing us, as the father of the prodigal kissed him when he returned a penitent. It is a kiss of peace. Kisses are opposed to wounds (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">Prov. xxvii. 6</reference>), so are the kisses of grace to the wounds of the law. Thus all true believers earnestly desire the manifestations of Christ's love to their souls; they desire no more to make them happy than the assurance of his favour, the lifting up of the light of his countenance upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>), and the knowledge of that love of his which surpasses knowledge; this is the one thing they desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. They are ready to welcome the manifestation of Christ's love to their souls by his Spirit, and to return them in the humble professions of love to him and complacency in him, above all. <hi type="italic">The fruit of his lips is peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa. lvii. 19</reference>. "Let him give me ten thousand kisses whose very fruition makes me desire him more, and, whereas all other pleasures sour and wither by using, those of the Spirit become more delightful." So bishop Reynolds. She gives several reasons for this desire. (1.) Because of the great esteem she has for his love: <hi type="italic">Thy love is better than wine.</hi> Wine <hi type="italic">makes glad the heart,</hi> revives the drooping spirits, and exhilarates them, but gracious souls take more pleasure in loving Christ and being beloved of him, in the fruits and gifts of his love and in the pledges and assurances of it, than any man ever took in the most exquisite delights of sense, and it is more reviving to them than ever the richest cordial was to one ready to faint. Note, [1.] Christ's love is in itself, and in the account of all the saints, more valuable and desirable than the best entertainments this world can give. [2.] Those only may expect the kisses of Christ's mouth, and the comfortable tokens of his favour, who prefer his love before all delights of the children of men, who would rather forego those delights than forfeit his favour, and take more pleasure in spiritual joys than in any bodily refreshments whatsoever. Observe here the change of the person: <hi type="italic">Let him kiss me;</hi> there she speaks of him as absent, or as if she were afraid to speak to him; but, in the next words, she sees him near at hand, and therefore directs her speech to him: "<hi type="italic">Thy love, thy loves</hi>" (so the word is), "I so earnestly desire, because I highly esteem it." (2.) Because of the diffuse fragrancy of his love and the fruits of it (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because of the savour of thy good ointment</hi> (the agreeableness and acceptableness of thy graces and comforts to all that rightly understand both them and themselves), <hi type="italic">thy name is as ointment poured forth,</hi> thou art so, and all that whereby thou hast made thyself known; thy very name is precious to all the saints; it is an ointment and perfume which rejoice the heart." The unfolding of Christ's name is as the opening of a box of precious ointment, which the room is filled with the odour of. The preaching of his gospel was the <hi type="italic">manifesting the savour of his knowledge in every place,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. The Spirit was the <hi type="italic">oil of gladness</hi> wherewith Christ was anointed (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">Heb. i. 9</reference>), and all true believers have that <hi type="italic">unction</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1 John ii. 27</reference>), so that he is precious to them, and they to him and to one another. <hi type="italic">A good name</hi> is <hi type="italic">as precious ointment,</hi> but Christ's name is more fragrant than any other. Wisdom, like oil, <hi type="italic">makes the face to shine;</hi> but the Redeemer outshines, in beauty, all others. The name of Christ is not now like ointment sealed up, as it had been long (<hi type="italic">Ask not after my name, for it is secret</hi>), but like <hi type="italic">ointment poured forth,</hi> which denotes both the freeness and fulness of the communications of his grace by the gospel. (3.) Because of the general affection that all holy souls have to him: <hi type="italic">Therefore do the virgins love thee.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">Christ's love shed abroad in our hearts</hi> that draws them out in love to him; all that are pure from the corruptions of sin, that preserve the chastity of their own spirits, and are true to the vows by which they have devoted themselves to God, that not only suffer not their affections to be violated but cannot bear so much as to be solicited by the world and the flesh, those are the virgins that love Jesus Christ and <hi type="italic">follow him whithersoever he goes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. And, because Christ is the darling of all the <hi type="italic">pure in heart,</hi> let him be ours, and let our desires be towards him and towards the <hi type="italic">kisses of his mouth.</hi> <div eID="gen15183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> 2. The bridegroom's fellowship, <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">v. 4</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen15184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> (1.) Her petition for divine grace: <hi type="italic">Draw me.</hi> This implies sense of distance from him, desire of union with him. "Draw me to thyself, draw me nearer, draw me home to thee." She had prayed that he would draw nigh to her (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">v. 2</reference>); in order to that, she prays that he would draw her nigh to him. "<hi type="italic">Draw me,</hi> not only with the moral suasion which there is in the fragrancy of the good ointments, not only with the attractives of that name which is as ointment poured forth, but with supernatural grace, with the <hi type="italic">cords of a man</hi> and the <hi type="italic">bands of love,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos. xi. 4</reference>. Christ has told us that none come to him but such as the Father draws, <reference osisRef="John.6.44">John vi. 44</reference>. We are not only weak, and cannot come of ourselves any further than we are helped, but we are naturally backward and averse to come, and therefore must pray for those influences and operations of the Spirit, by the power of which we are unwilling made willing, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Draw me,</hi> else I move not; overpower the world and the flesh that would draw me from thee." We are not driven to Christ, but drawn in such a way as is agreeable to rational creatures. <div eID="gen15185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> (2.) Her promise to improve that grace: <hi type="italic">Draw me,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">we will run after thee.</hi> See how the doctrine of special and effectual grace consists with our duty, and is a powerful engagement and encouragement to it, and yet reserves all the glory of all the good that is in us to God only. Observe, [1.] The flowing forth of the soul after Christ, and its ready compliance with him, are the effect of his grace; we could not run after him if he did not draw us, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2 Cor. iii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.13">Phil. iv. 13</reference>. [2.] The grace which God gives us we must diligently improve. When Christ by his Spirit draws us we must with our spirits run after him. As God says, <hi type="italic">I will,</hi> and <hi type="italic">you shall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.27">Ezek. xxxvi. 27</reference>), so we must say, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt</hi> and <hi type="italic">we will;</hi> thou shalt <hi type="italic">work in us both to will and to do,</hi> and therefore we will work out our own salvation" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.12-Phil.2.13">Phil. ii. 12, 13</reference>); not only we will walk, but we will run after thee, which denotes eagerness of desire, readiness of affection, vigour of pursuit, and swiftness of motion. <hi type="italic">When thou shalt enlarge my heart</hi> then <hi type="italic">I will run the way of thy commandments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Ps. cxix. 32</reference>); when <hi type="italic">thy right hand upholds me</hi> then <hi type="italic">my soul follows hard after thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Ps. lxiii. 8</reference>); when with lovingkindness to us he draws us (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>) we with lovingkindness to him must run after him, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa. xl. 31</reference>. Observe the difference between the petition and the promise: "Draw me, and then we will run." When Christ pours out his Spirit upon the church in general, which is his bride, all the members of it do thence receive enlivening quickening influences, and are made to run to him with the more cheerfulness, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa. lv. 5</reference>. Or, "Draw me" (says the believing soul) "and then I will not only follow thee myself as fast as I can, but will bring all mine along with me: <hi type="italic">We will run after thee,</hi> I and the <hi type="italic">virgins that love thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">v. 3</reference>), I and all that I have any interest in or influence upon, <hi type="italic">I and my house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>), I and the <hi type="italic">transgressors whom I will teach thy ways,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.51.13">Ps. li. 13</reference>. Those that put themselves forth, in compliance with divine grace, shall find that their <hi type="italic">zeal will provoke many,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2 Cor. ix. 2</reference>. Those that are lively will be active; when Philip was drawn to Christ he drew Nathanael; and they will be exemplary, and so will win those that would not be won by the word. <div eID="gen15186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15187" type="x-p"/> (3.) The immediate answer that was given to this prayer: <hi type="italic">The King has</hi> drawn me, has <hi type="italic">brought me into his chambers.</hi> It is not so much an answer fetched by faith from the world of Christ's grace as an answer fetched by experience from the workings of his grace. If we observe, as we ought, the returns of prayer, we may find that sometimes, <hi type="italic">while we are yet speaking,</hi> Christ hears, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>. The bridegroom is a king; so much the more wonderful is his condescension in the invitations and entertainments that he gives us, and so much the greater reason have we to accept of them and to <hi type="italic">run after him.</hi> God is the King that has made the <hi type="italic">marriage-supper</hi> for his Son (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">Matt. xxii. 2</reference>) and brings in even <hi type="italic">the poor and the maimed,</hi> and even the most shy and bashful are <hi type="italic">compelled to come in.</hi> Those that are drawn to Christ are brought, not only into his courts, into his palaces (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">Ps. xlv. 15</reference>), but into his presence-chamber, where his secret is with them (<reference osisRef="John.14.21">John xiv. 21</reference>), and where they are safe in his pavilion, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Ps. xxvii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa. xxvi. 20</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">wait at wisdom's gates</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">made to come</hi> (so the word is) <hi type="italic">into her chambers;</hi> they shall be led into truth and comfort. <div eID="gen15187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15188" type="x-p"/> (4.) The wonderful complacency which the spouse takes in the honour which the king put upon her. Being <hi type="italic">brought into the chamber,</hi> [1.] "We have what we would have. Our desires are crowned with unspeakable delights; all our griefs vanish, and <hi type="italic">we will be glad and rejoice.</hi> If <hi type="italic">a day in the courts,</hi> much more an hour in the chambers, <hi type="italic">is better than a thousand,</hi> than ten thousand, elsewhere." Those that are, through grace, brought into covenant and communion with God, have reason to <hi type="italic">go on their way rejoicing,</hi> as the eunuch (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">Acts viii. 39</reference>), and that joy will enlarge our hearts and be our strength, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>. [2.] All our joy shall centre in God: "<hi type="italic">We will rejoice,</hi> not in the ointments, or the chambers, but <hi type="italic">in thee.</hi> It is God only that is our <hi type="italic">exceeding joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Ps. xliii. 4</reference>. We have no joy but in Christ, and which we are indebted to him for." <hi type="italic">Gaudium in Domino</hi>—<hi type="italic">Joy in the Lord,</hi> was the ancient salutation, and <hi type="italic">Salus in Domino sempiterna</hi>—<hi type="italic">Eternal salvation in the Lord.</hi> [3.] "We will retain the relish and savour of this kindness of thine and never forget it: <hi type="italic">We will remember thy loves more than wine;</hi> no only thy love itself (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">v. 2</reference>), but the very remembrance of it shall be more grateful to us than the strongest cordial to the spirits, or the most palatable liquor to the taste. We will remember to give thanks for thy love, and it shall make more durable impressions upon us than any thing in this world." <div eID="gen15188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15189" type="x-p"/> (5.) The communion which a gracious soul has with all the saints in this communion with Christ. In the chambers to which we are brought we not only meet with him, but meet with one another (<reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1 John i. 7</reference>); for <hi type="italic">the upright love thee;</hi> the congregation, the generation, of the <hi type="italic">upright love thee.</hi> Whatever others do, all that are Israelites indeed, and faithful to God, will love Jesus Christ. Whatever differences of apprehension and affection there may be among Christians in other things, this they are all agreed in, Jesus Christ is precious to them. <hi type="italic">The upright</hi> here are the same with the <hi type="italic">virgins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.1.3">v. 3</reference>. All that <hi type="italic">remember his love more than wine</hi> will love him with a superlative love. Nor is any love acceptable to Christ but the love of <hi type="italic">the upright,</hi> love in sincerity, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.24">Eph. vi. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen15189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15190" type="x-p"/> II. To <hi type="italic">the daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.1.5-Song.1.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. The church in general, being in distress, speaks to particular churches to guard them against the danger they were in of being offended at the church's sufferings, <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1 Thess. iii. 3</reference>. Or the believer speaks to those that were professors at large in the church, but not of it, or to weak Christians, babes in Christ, that labour under much ignorance, infirmity, and mistake, not perfectly instructed, and yet willing to be taught in the things of God. She observed these by-standers look disdainfully upon her because of her blackness, in respect both of sins and sufferings, upon the account of which they though she had little reason to expect the kisses she wished for (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">v. 2</reference>) or to expect that they should join with her in her joys, <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">v. 4</reference>. She therefore endeavors to remove this offence; she owns she is <hi type="italic">black.</hi> Guilt blackens; the heresies, scandals, and offences, that happen in the church, make her <hi type="italic">black;</hi> and the best saints have their failings. Sorrow blackens; that seems to be especially meant; the church is often in a low condition, mean, and poor, and in appearance despicable, her beauty sullied and her face foul with weeping; she is in mourning weeds, clothed with sackcloth, as the Nazarites that had become <hi type="italic">blacker than a coal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.8">Lam. iv. 8</reference>. Now, to take off this offence, <div eID="gen15190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15191" type="x-p"/> 1. She asserts her own comeliness notwithstanding (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am black, but comely,</hi> black <hi type="italic">as the tents of Kedar,</hi> in which the shepherds lived, which were very coarse, and never whitened, weather-beaten and discoloured by long use, but comely <hi type="italic">as the curtains of Solomon,</hi> the furniture of whose rooms, no doubt, was sumptuous and rich, in proportion to the stateliness of his houses. The church is sometimes <hi type="italic">black</hi> with persecution, <hi type="italic">but comely</hi> in patience, constancy, and consolation, and never the less amiable in the eyes of Christ, <hi type="italic">black in the account of men, but comely</hi> in God's esteem, <hi type="italic">black</hi> in some that are a scandal to her, <hi type="italic">but comely</hi> in others that are sincere and are an honour to her. True believers are <hi type="italic">black</hi> in themselves, <hi type="italic">but comely</hi> in Christ, with the comeliness that he puts upon them, <hi type="italic">black</hi> outwardly, for <hi type="italic">the world knows them not,</hi> but <hi type="italic">all glorious within,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Ps. xlv. 13</reference>. St. Paul was <hi type="italic">weak,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">strong,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">2 Cor. xii. 10</reference>. And so the church is <hi type="italic">black</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">comely;</hi> a believer is a sinner and yet a saint; his own righteousnesses are <hi type="italic">as filthy rags,</hi> but he is clothed with the robe of Christ's righteousness. The Chaldee Paraphrase applies it to the people of Israel's blackness when they made the golden calf and their comeliness when they repented of it. <div eID="gen15191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15192" type="x-p"/> 2. She gives an account how she came to be so black. The blackness was not natural, but contracted, and was owing to the hard usage that had been given her: <hi type="italic">Look not upon me</hi> so scornfully <hi type="italic">because I am black.</hi> We must take heed with what eye we look upon the church, especially when she is in black. <hi type="italic">Thou shouldst not have looked upon the day of thy brother,</hi> the day of his affliction, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.12">Obad. 12</reference>. Be not offended; for, <div eID="gen15192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15193" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">I am black</hi> by reason of my sufferings: <hi type="italic">The sun has looked upon me.</hi> She was fair and comely; whiteness was her proper colour; but she got this blackness by <hi type="italic">the burden and heat of the day,</hi> which she was forced to bear. She was sun-burnt, scorched with tribulation and persecution (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.6">Matt. xiii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.21">21</reference>); and the greatest beauties, if exposed to the weather, are soonest tanned. Observe how she mitigates her troubles; she does not say, as Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Gen. xxxi. 40</reference>), <hi type="italic">In the day the drought consumed me,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">The sun has looked upon me;</hi> for it becomes not God's suffering people to make the worst of their sufferings. But what was the matter? [1.] She fell under the displeasure of those of her own house: <hi type="italic">My mother's children were angry with me.</hi> She was <hi type="italic">in perils by false brethren;</hi> her foes were <hi type="italic">those of her own house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">Matt. x. 36</reference>), brethren by nature as men, by profession as members of the same sacred corporation, the children of the church her mother, but not of God her Father; they <hi type="italic">were angry with</hi> her. The Samaritans, who claimed kindred to the Jews, were vexed at any thing that tended to the prosperity of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">Neh. ii. 10</reference>. Note, It is no new thing for the people of God to fall under the anger of their own mother's children. <hi type="italic">It was thou, a man, my equal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.12-Ps.55.13">Ps. lv. 12, 13</reference>. This makes the trouble the more irksome and grievous; from such it is taken unkindly, and the anger of such is implacable. <hi type="italic">A brother offended is hard to be won.</hi> [2.] They dealt very hardly with her: <hi type="italic">They made me the keeper of the vineyards,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "They seduced me to sin, drew me into false worships, to serve their gods, which was like dressing the vineyards, <hi type="italic">keeping the vine of Sodom;</hi> and they would not let me <hi type="italic">keep my own vineyard,</hi> serve my own God, and observe those pure worships which he gave me in charge, and which I do and ever will own for mine." These are grievances which good people complain most of in a time of persecution, that their consciences are forced, and that those who rule them with rigour say <hi type="italic">to their souls, Bow down, that we may go over,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Isa. li. 23</reference>. Or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "They brought me into trouble, imposed that upon me which was toilsome, and burdensome, and very disgraceful." Keeping the vineyards was base servile work, and very laborious, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.5">Isa. lxi. 5</reference>. Her mother's children made her the drudge of the family. <hi type="italic">Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, and their wrath, for it was cruel.</hi> The spouse of Christ has met with a great deal of hard usage. <div eID="gen15193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15194" type="x-p"/> (2.) "My sufferings are such as I have deserved; for <hi type="italic">my own vineyard have I not kept.</hi> How unrighteous soever my brethren are in persecuting me, God is righteous in permitting them to do so. I am justly made a slavish keeper of men's vineyards, because I have been a careless keeper of the vineyards God has entrusted me with." Slothful servants of God are justly made to serve their enemies, <hi type="italic">that they may know his service, and the service of the kings of the countries,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2 Chron. xii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.47-Deut.28.48">Deut. xxviii. 47, 48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.23-Ezek.20.24">Ezek. xx. 23, 24</reference>. "Think not the worse of the ways of God for my sufferings, for I smart for my own folly." Note, When God's people are oppressed and persecuted it becomes them to acknowledge their own sin to be the procuring cause of their troubles, especially their carelessness in keeping their vineyards, so that it has been like <hi type="italic">the field of the slothful.</hi>
entries.5f3b6cfaa426dbd094bc67853b79e01151ae81d7: <div eID="gen15194" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou makest <hi type="italic">thy flock</hi> to rest at noon: for why should I be as one that turneth aside by the flocks of thy companions? <hi type="super">8</hi> If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds' tents. <hi type="super">9</hi> I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh's chariots. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thy cheeks are comely with rows <hi type="italic">of jewels,</hi> thy neck with chains <hi type="italic">of gold.</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> We will make thee borders of gold with studs of silver. <div eID="gen15195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15196" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The humble petition which the spouse presents to her beloved, the shepherdess to the shepherd, the church and every believer to Christ, for a more free and intimate communion with him. She turns from the <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> to whom she had complained both of her sins and of her troubles, and looks up to heaven for relief and succour against both, <reference osisRef="Song.1.7">v. 7</reference>. Here observe, 1. The title she gives to Christ: <hi type="italic">O thou whom my soul loveth.</hi> Note, It is the undoubted character of all true believers that their souls love Jesus Christ, which intimates both the sincerity and the strength of their love; they <hi type="italic">love him with all their hearts;</hi> and those that do so may come to him boldly and may humbly plead it with him. 2. The opinion she has of him as the good shepherd of the sheep; she doubts not but he <hi type="italic">feeds his flock</hi> and <hi type="italic">makes them rest at noon.</hi> Jesus Christ graciously provides both repast and repose for his sheep; they are not starved, but well fed, not scattered upon the mountains, but fed together, fed <hi type="italic">in green pastures</hi> and in the hot time of the day <hi type="italic">led by the still waters</hi> and made to lie down under a cool refreshing shade. Is it with God's people a noon-time of outward troubles, inward conflicts? Christ has rest for them; he <hi type="italic">carries them in his arms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>. 3. Her request to him that she might be admitted into his society: <hi type="italic">Tell me where thou feedest.</hi> Those that would be told, that would be taught, what they are concerned to know and do, must apply to Jesus Christ, and beg of him to teach them, to tell them. "Tell me where to find thee, where I may have conversation with thee, <hi type="italic">where thou feedest</hi> and tendest thy flock, that there I may have some of my company." Observe, by the way, We should not, in love to our friends and their company, tempt them or urge them to neglect their business, but desire such an enjoyment of them as will consist with it, and rather, if we can, to join with them in their business and help to forward it. "<hi type="italic">Tell me where thou feedest,</hi> and there I will sit with thee, walk with thee, feed my flocks with thine, and not hinder thee nor myself, but bring my work with me." Note, Those whose souls love Jesus Christ earnestly desire to have communion with him, by his word in which he speaks to us and by prayer in which we speak to him, and to share in the privileges of his flock; and we may learn from the care he takes of his church, to provide convenient food and rest for it, how to take care of our own souls, which are our charge. 4. The plea she uses for the enforcing of this request: "<hi type="italic">For why should I be as one that turns aside by</hi> (or after) <hi type="italic">the flocks of thy companions,</hi> that pretend to be so, but are really thy competitors, and rivals with thee." Note, Turning aside from Christ after other lovers is that which gracious souls dread, and deprecate, more than any thing else. "Thou wouldst not have me to <hi type="italic">turn aside,</hi> no, nor to <hi type="italic">be as one that turns aside;</hi> <hi type="italic">tell me</hi> then, O tell me, where I may be near thee, and I will never leave thee." (1.) "<hi type="italic">Why should I</hi> lie under suspicion, and look as if I belonged to some other and not to thee? <hi type="italic">Why should I be</hi> thought <hi type="italic">by the flocks of our companions</hi> to be a deserter from thee, and a retainer to some other shepherd?" Good Christians will be afraid of giving any occasion to those about them to question their faith in Christ and their love to him; they would not do any thing that looks like unconcernedness about their souls; or uncharitableness towards their brethren, or that savours of indifference and disaffection to holy ordinances; and we should pray to God to direct us into and keep us in the way of our duty, that we may not so much as <hi type="italic">seem to come short,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.1">Heb. iv. 1</reference>. (2.) "<hi type="italic">Why should I</hi> lie in temptation to <hi type="italic">turn aside,</hi> as I do while I am absent from thee?" We should be earnest with God for a settled peace in communion with God through Christ, that we may not be as waifs and strays, ready to be picked up by him that next passes by. <div eID="gen15196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15197" type="x-p"/> II. The gracious answer which the bridegroom gives to this request, <reference osisRef="Song.1.8">v. 8</reference>. See how ready God is to answer prayer, especially prayers for instruction; even while she is yet speaking, he hears. Observe, 1. How affectionately he speaks to her: <hi type="italic">O thou fairest among women!</hi> Note, Believing souls are fair, in the eyes of the Lord Jesus, above any other. Christ sees a beauty in holiness, whether we do or no. The spouse has called herself black, but Christ calls her fair. Those that are low in their own eyes are so much the more amiable in the eyes of Jesus Christ. Blushing at their own deformity (says Mr. Durham) is a chief part of their beauty. 2. How mildly he checks her for her ignorance, in these words, <hi type="italic">If thou know not,</hi> intimating that she might have known it if it had not been her own fault. What! dost thou not know where to find me and my flock? Compare Christ's answer to a like address of Philip's (<reference osisRef="John.14.9">John xiv. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip?</hi> But, 3. With what tenderness he acquaints her where she might find him. If men say, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ, or, Lo, he is there, believe them not, go not after them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.23">Matt. xxiv. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.26">26</reference>. But, (1.) <hi type="italic">Walk in the way of good men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">Prov. ii. 20</reference>), follow the track, ask for the good old way, observe <hi type="italic">the footsteps of the flock,</hi> and <hi type="italic">go forth by</hi> them. It will not serve to sit still and cry, "Lord, show me the way," but we must bestir ourselves to enquire out the way; and we may find it by looking which way <hi type="italic">the footsteps of the flock</hi> lead, what has been the practice of godly people all along; let that practice be ours, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">Heb. vi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1 Cor. xi. 1</reference>. (2.) Sit under the direction of good ministers: "<hi type="italic">Feed</hi> thyself <hi type="italic">and thy kids besides the tents of the under-shepherds.</hi> Bring thy charge with thee" (it is probable that the custom was to commit the lambs and kids to the custody of the women, the shepherdesses); "they shall all be welcome; <hi type="italic">the shepherds</hi> will be no hindrance to thee, as they were to Reuel's daughters (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.17">Exod. ii. 17</reference>), but helpers rather, and therefore abide by their tents." Note, Those that would have acquaintance and communion with Christ must closely and conscientiously adhere to holy ordinances, must join themselves to his people and attend his ministers. Those that have the charge of families must bring them with them to religious assemblies; let their <hi type="italic">kids,</hi> their children, their servants, have the benefit of <hi type="italic">the shepherds' tents.</hi> <div eID="gen15197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15198" type="x-p"/> III. The high encomiums which the bridegroom gives of his spouse. To be <hi type="italic">given in marriage,</hi> in the Hebrew dialect, is to be <hi type="italic">praised</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.63">Ps. lxxviii. 63</reference>, margin), so this spouse is here; her <hi type="italic">husband praises</hi> this <hi type="italic">virtuous woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.28">Prov. xxxi. 28</reference>); he praises her, as is usual in poems, by similitudes. 1. He calls her his <hi type="italic">love</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">v. 9</reference>); it is an endearing compellation often used in this book: "My friend, my companion, my familiar." 2. He compares her to a set of strong and stately <hi type="italic">horses in Pharaoh's chariots.</hi> Egypt was famous for the best horses. Solomon had his thence; and Pharaoh, no doubt, had the choicest the country afforded for his own chariots. The church had complained of her own weakness, and the danger she was in of being made a prey of by her enemies: "Fear not," says Christ; "<hi type="italic">I have made thee like a company of horses;</hi> I have put strength into thee as I have done into <hi type="italic">the horse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.19">Job xxxix. 19</reference>), so that thou shalt with a gracious boldness <hi type="italic">mock at fear, and not be affrighted,</hi> like <hi type="italic">the lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord has made thee as his goodly horse in the day of battle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zech. x. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">I have compared thee to my company of horses</hi> which triumphed over <hi type="italic">Pharaoh's chariots,</hi> the holy angels, <hi type="italic">horses of fire.</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hab.3.15">Hab. iii. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou didst walk through the sea with thy horses;</hi> and see <reference osisRef="Isa.63.13">Isa. lxiii. 13</reference>. We are weak in ourselves, but if Christ make us as horses, strong and bold, we need not fear what all the powers of darkness can do against us. 3. He admires the beauty and ornaments of her countenance (<reference osisRef="Song.1.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels,</hi> the attire of the head, curls of hair, or favourites (so some), or knots of ribbons; <hi type="italic">thy neck also with chains,</hi> such as persons of the first rank wear, <hi type="italic">chains of gold.</hi> The ordinances of Christ are the ornaments of the church. The graces, gifts, and comforts of the Spirit, are the adorning of every believing soul, and beautify it; these render it, <hi type="italic">in the sight of God, of great price.</hi> The ornaments of the saints are many, but all orderly disposed in <hi type="italic">rows</hi> and <hi type="italic">chains,</hi> in which there is a mutual connexion with and dependence upon each other. The beauty is not from any thing in themselves, from the <hi type="italic">neck</hi> or from the <hi type="italic">cheeks,</hi> but from ornaments with which they are set off. It was <hi type="italic">comeliness which I put upon thee, said the Lord God;</hi> for we were born not only naked, but polluted, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Ezek. xvi. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen15198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15199" type="x-p"/> IV. His gracious purpose to add to her ornaments; for where God has given true grace he will give more grace; <hi type="italic">to him that has shall be given.</hi> Is the church courageous in her resistance of sin, as the <hi type="italic">horses in Pharaoh's chariots?</hi> Is she <hi type="italic">comely</hi> in the exercise of grace, as <hi type="italic">with rows of jewels</hi> and <hi type="italic">chains of gold?</hi> She shall be yet further beautified (<reference osisRef="Song.1.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">We will make thee borders of gold,</hi> inlaid, or enamelled, <hi type="italic">with studs of silver.</hi> Whatever is wanting shall be made up, till the church and every true believer come to be <hi type="italic">perfect in beauty;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Ezek. xvi. 14</reference>. This is here undertaken to be done by the concurring power of the three persons in the Godhead: <hi type="italic">We will</hi> do it; like that (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Gen. i. 26</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Let us make man;</hi> so let us new-make him, and perfect his beauty." The same that is the author will be the finisher of the good work; and it cannot miscarry.
entries.b8932c50bb59fd7a4081ea1474743e27bcd989e8: <div eID="gen15199" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conference between Christ and His Church.</title> <div sID="gen15200" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> While the king <hi type="italic">sitteth</hi> at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof. <hi type="super">13</hi> A bundle of myrrh <hi type="italic">is</hi> my wellbeloved unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts. <hi type="super">14</hi> My beloved <hi type="italic">is</hi> unto me <hi type="italic">as</hi> a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi. <hi type="super">15</hi> Behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> fair, my love; behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> fair; thou <hi type="italic">hast</hi> doves' eyes. <hi type="super">16</hi> Behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: also our bed <hi type="italic">is</hi> green. <hi type="super">17</hi> The beams of our house <hi type="italic">are</hi> cedar, <hi type="italic">and</hi> our rafters of fir. <div eID="gen15200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15201" type="x-p"/> Here the conference is carried on between Christ and his spouse, and endearments are mutually exchanged. <div eID="gen15201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15202" type="x-p"/> I. Believers take a great complacency in Christ, and in communion with him. <hi type="italic">To you that believe he is precious,</hi> above any thing in this world, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1 Pet. ii. 7</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen15202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15203" type="x-p"/> 1. The humble reverence believers have for Christ as their Sovereign, <reference osisRef="Song.1.12">v. 12</reference>. He is a <hi type="italic">King</hi> in respect both of dignity and dominion; he wears the crown of honour, he bears the sceptre of power, both which are the unspeakable satisfaction of all his people. This King has his royal table spread in the gospel, in which is <hi type="italic">made for all nations a feast of fat things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>. Wisdom has <hi type="italic">furnished her table,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Prov. ix. 1</reference>. He <hi type="italic">sits at this table</hi> to <hi type="italic">see his guests</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.11">Matt. xxii. 11</reference>), to see that nothing be wanting that is fit for them; he <hi type="italic">sups with them</hi> and <hi type="italic">they with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Rev. iii. 20</reference>); he has fellowship with them and rejoices in them; he <hi type="italic">sits at his table</hi> to bid them welcome, and to carve for them, as Christ <hi type="italic">broke the five loaves</hi> and gave to his disciples, that they might distribute to the multitude. He sits there to receive petitions, as Ahasuerus admitted Esther's petition at <hi type="italic">the banquet of wine.</hi> He has promised to be present with his people in his ordinances always. Then believers do him all the honour they can, and study how to express their esteem of him and gratitude to him, as Mary did when she anointed his head with <hi type="italic">the ointment of spikenard</hi> that was <hi type="italic">very costly,</hi> one pound of it worth <hi type="italic">three hundred pence,</hi> and so fragrant that <hi type="italic">the house was filled with the pleasing odour of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.3">John xii. 3</reference>), which story seems as if it were designed to refer to this passage, for Christ was then <hi type="italic">sitting at table.</hi> When good Christians, in any religious duty, especially in the ordinance of the Lord's supper, where the King is pleased, as it were, to <hi type="italic">sit</hi> with us <hi type="italic">at his</hi> own <hi type="italic">table,</hi> have their graces exercised, their hearts broken by repentance, healed by faith, and inflamed with holy love and desires toward Christ, with joyful expectations of the glory to be revealed, then the <hi type="italic">spikenard sends forth the smell thereof.</hi> Christ is pleased to reckon himself honoured by it, and to accept of it as an instance of respect to him, as it was in the wise men of the east, who paid their homage to the new-born King of the Jews by presenting to him <hi type="italic">frankincense and myrrh.</hi> The graces of God's Spirit in the hearts of believers are exceedingly precious in themselves and pleasing to Christ, and his presence in ordinances draws them out into act and exercise. If he withdraw, graces wither and languish, as plants in the absence of the sun; if he approach, the face of the soul is renewed, as of the earth in the spring; and then it is time to bestir ourselves, that we may not lose the gleam, not lose the gale; for nothing is done acceptably but what grace does, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">Heb. xii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen15203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15204" type="x-p"/> 2. The strong affection they have for Christ as their <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> their <hi type="italic">well-beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.1.13">v. 13</reference>. Christ is not only <hi type="italic">beloved</hi> by all believing souls, but is their <hi type="italic">well-beloved,</hi> their best-beloved, their only beloved; he has that place in their hearts which no rival can be admitted to, the innermost and uppermost place. Observe, (1.) How Christ is accounted of by all believers: He is <hi type="italic">a bundle of myrrh</hi> and <hi type="italic">a cluster of camphire,</hi> something, we may be sure, nay, every thing, that is pleasant and delightful. The doctrine of his gospel, and the comforts of his Spirit, are very refreshing to them, and they rest in his love; none of all the delights of sense are comparable to the spiritual pleasure they have in meditating on Christ and enjoying him. There is a complicated sweetness in Christ and an abundance of it; there is <hi type="italic">a bundle of myrrh</hi> and <hi type="italic">a cluster of camphire.</hi> We are not straitened in him whom there is <hi type="italic">all fulness.</hi> The word translated <hi type="italic">camphire</hi> is <hi type="italic">copher,</hi> the same word that signifies <hi type="italic">atonement</hi> or <hi type="italic">propitiation.</hi> Christ is <hi type="italic">a cluster</hi> of merit and righteousness to all believers; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he is dear to them because <hi type="italic">he is the propitiation for their sins.</hi> Observe what stress the spouse lays upon the application: He <hi type="italic">is unto me,</hi> and again <hi type="italic">unto me,</hi> all that is sweet; whatever he is to others, he is so <hi type="italic">to me.</hi> He <hi type="italic">loved me, and gave himself for me.</hi> He <hi type="italic">is my Lord, and my God.</hi> (2.) How he is accepted: <hi type="italic">He shall lie all night between my breasts,</hi> near my heart. Christ lays the beloved disciples in his bosom; why then should not they lay their beloved Saviour in their bosoms? Why should not they embrace him with both arms, and hold him fast, with a resolution never to let him go? Christ must <hi type="italic">dwell in the heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Eph. iii. 17</reference>), and, in order to that, the adulteries must be put from <hi type="italic">between the breasts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.2">Hos. ii. 2</reference>), no pretender must have his place in the soul. He shall be as <hi type="italic">a bundle of myrrh,</hi> or perfume bag, between <hi type="italic">my breasts,</hi> always sweet to me; or his effigies in miniature, his love-tokens, shall be hung between <hi type="italic">my breasts,</hi> according to the custom of those that are dear to each other. He shall not only be laid their for a while, but shall lie there, shall abide there. <div eID="gen15204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15205" type="x-p"/> II. Jesus Christ has a great complacency in his church and in every true believer; they are amiable in his eyes (<reference osisRef="Song.1.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, thou art fair, my love;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Behold, thou art fair.</hi> He says this, not to make her proud (humility is one principal ingredient in spiritual beauty), but, 1. To show that there is a real beauty in holiness, that all who are sanctified are thereby beautified; they are truly fair. 2. That he takes great delight in that good work which his grace has wrought on the souls of believers; so that though they have their infirmities, whatever they think of themselves, and the world thinks of them, he thinks them fair. He calls them friends. The <hi type="italic">hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible,</hi> is <hi type="italic">in the sight of God of great price,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1 Pet. iii. 4</reference>. 3. To comfort weak believers, who are discouraged by their own blackness; let them be told again and again that they are fair. 4. To engage all who are sanctified to be very thankful for that grace which has made them fair, who by nature were deformed, and changed the Ethiopian's skin. One instance of the beauty of the spouse is here mentioned, that she <hi type="italic">has doves' eyes,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">ch. iv. 1</reference>. Those are fair, in Christ's account, who have, not the piercing eye of the eagle, but the pure and chaste eye of the <hi type="italic">dove,</hi> not like the hawk, who, when he soars upwards, still has his eye upon the prey on earth, but a humble modest eye, such an eye as discovers a simplicity and godly sincerity and a dove-like innocency, eyes enlightened and guided by the Holy Spirit, that blessed Dove, weeping eyes. I did <hi type="italic">mourn as a dove,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Ezek. vii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen15205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15206" type="x-p"/> III. The church expresses her value for Christ, and returns esteem (<reference osisRef="Song.1.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, thou art fair.</hi> See how Christ and believers praise one another. Israel saith of God, <hi type="italic">Who is like thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exod. xv. 11</reference>. And God saith of Israel, <hi type="italic">Who is like thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>. Lord, saith the church, "Dost thou call me <hi type="italic">fair?</hi> No; if we speak of strength, <hi type="italic">thou art strong</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job ix. 19</reference>), so, if of beauty, <hi type="italic">thou art fair.</hi> I am fair no otherwise than as I have thy image stamped upon me. Thou art the great Original; I am but a faint and imperfect copy, I am but thy <hi type="italic">umbra</hi>—<hi type="italic">the shadow of thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.34">iii. 34</reference>. Thou art fair in thyself and (which is more) <hi type="italic">pleasant</hi> to all that are thine. Many are fair enough to look at, and yet the sourness of their temper renders them unpleasant; but <hi type="italic">thou art fair, yea, pleasant.</hi>" Christ is pleasant, as he is ours, in covenant with us, in relation to us. "Thou art pleasant now, when the <hi type="italic">King sits at his table.</hi>" Christ is always precious to believers, but in a special manner pleasant when they are admitted into communion with him, when they hear his voice, and see his face, and taste his love. <hi type="italic">It is good to be here.</hi> Having expressed her esteem of her husband's person, she next, like a loving spouse, that is transported with joy for having disposed of herself so well, applauds the accommodations he had for her entertainment, his <hi type="italic">bed,</hi> his <hi type="italic">house,</hi> his <hi type="italic">rafters</hi> or <hi type="italic">galleries</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.16">v. 16</reference>), which may be fitly applied to those holy ordinances in which believers have fellowship with Jesus Christ, receive the tokens of his love and return their pious and devout affections to him, increase their acquaintance with him and improve their advantages by him. Now, 1. These she calls <hi type="italic">ours,</hi> Christ and believers having a joint-interest in them. As husband and wife are <hi type="italic">heirs together</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1 Pet. iii. 7</reference>), so believers are <hi type="italic">joint-heirs with Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Rom. viii. 17</reference>. They are his institutions and their privileges; in them Christ and believers meet. She does not call them <hi type="italic">mine,</hi> for a believer will own nothing as his but what Christ shall have an interest in, nor <hi type="italic">thine,</hi> for Christ has said, <hi type="italic">All that I have is thine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.15.31">Luke xv. 31</reference>. All is <hi type="italic">ours</hi> if we are Christ's. Those that can by faith lay claim to Christ may lay claim to all that is his. 2. These are the best of the kind. Does the colour of the bed, and the furniture belonging to it, help to set it off? <hi type="italic">Our bed is green,</hi> a colour which, in a pastoral, is preferred before any other, because it is the colour of the fields and groves where the shepherd's business and delight are. It is a refreshing colour, good for the eyes; and it denotes fruitfulness. <hi type="italic">I am like a green olive-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Ps. lii. 8</reference>. We are <hi type="italic">married to</hi> Christ, <hi type="italic">that we should bring forth unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">Rom. vii. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">The beams of our house are cedar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.17">v. 17</reference>), which probably refers to the temple Solomon had lately built for communion between God and Israel, which was of <hi type="italic">cedar,</hi> a strong sort of wood, sweet, durable, and which will never rot, typifying the firmness and continuance of the church, the gospel-temple. The galleries for walking are <hi type="italic">of fir,</hi> or <hi type="italic">cypress,</hi> some sort of wood that was pleasing both to the sight and to the smell, intimating the delight which the saints take in walking with Christ and conversing with him. Every thing in the covenant of grace (on which foot all their treaties are carried on) is very firm, very fine, and very fragrant.  <chapter eID="Song.1"/> <div eID="gen15206" type="x-p"/>

entries.d8746c1237226ae520e20acf948b9ff2a2dd6b0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8192"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> The Song of Solomon, called in the Vulgate and Septuagint, "The Song of Songs," from the opening words. This title denotes its superior excellence, according to the Hebrew idiom; so holy of holies, equivalent to "most holy" (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Ex 29:37</reference>); the heaven of heavens, equivalent to the highest heavens (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.14">De 10:14</reference>). It is one of the five volumes (megilloth) placed immediately after the Pentateuch in manuscripts of the Jewish Scriptures. It is also fourth of the Hagiographa (Cetubim, writings) or the third division of the Old Testament, the other two being the Law and the Prophets. The Jewish enumeration of the Cetubim is Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra (including Nehemiah), and Chronicles. Its canonicity is certain; it is found in all Hebrew manuscripts of Scripture; also in the Greek Septuagint; in the catalogues of Melito, bishop of Sardis, A.D. 170 (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, 4.26), and of others of the ancient Church.<div eID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> Origen and Jerome tell us that the Jews forbade it to be read by any until he was thirty years old. It certainly needs a degree of spiritual maturity to enter aright into the holy mystery of love which it allegorically sets forth. To such as have attained this maturity, of whatever age they be, the Song of Songs is one of the most edifying of the sacred writings. Rosenmuller justly says, The sudden transitions of the bride from the court to the grove are inexplicable, on the supposition that it describes merely human love. Had it been the latter, it would have been positively objectionable, and never would have been inserted in the holy canon. The allusion to "Pharaoh's chariots" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>) has been made a ground for conjecturing that the love of Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter is the subject of the Song. But this passage alludes to a remarkable event in the history of the Old Testament Church, the deliverance from the hosts and chariots of Pharaoh at the Red Sea. (However, see on <reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>). The other allusions are quite opposed to the notion; the bride is represented at times as a shepherdess (<reference osisRef="Song.1.7">So 1:7</reference>), "an abomination to the Egyptians" (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.34">Ge 46:34</reference>); so also <reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">5:7</reference> are at variance with it. The Christian fathers, Origen and Theodoret, compared the teachings of Solomon to a ladder with three steps; Ecclesiastes, natural (the nature of sensible things, vain); Proverbs, moral; Canticles, mystical (figuring the union of Christ and the Church). The Jews compared Proverbs to the outer court of Solomon's temple, Ecclesiastes to the holy place, and Canticles to the holy of holies. Understood allegorically, the Song is cleared of all difficulty. "Shulamith" (<reference osisRef="Song.6.13">So 6:13</reference>), the bride, is thus an appropriate name, Daughter of Peace being the feminine of Solomon, equivalent to the Prince of Peace. She by turns is a vinedresser, shepherdess, midnight inquirer, and prince's consort and daughter, and He a suppliant drenched with night dews, and a king in His palace, in harmony with the various relations of the Church and Christ. As Ecclesiastes sets forth the vanity of love of the creature, Canticles sets forth the fullness of the love which joins believers and the Saviour. The entire economy of salvation, says Harris, aims at restoring to the world the lost spirit of love. God is love, and Christ is the embodiment of the love of God. As the other books of Scripture present severally their own aspects of divine truth, so Canticles furnishes the believer with language of holy love, wherewith his heart can commune with his Lord; and it portrays the intensity of Christ's love to him; the affection of love was created in man to be a transcript of the divine love, and the Song clothes the latter in words; were it not for this, we should be at a loss for language, having the divine warrant, wherewith to express, without presumption, the fervor of the love between Christ and us. The image of a bride, a bridegroom, and a marriage, to represent this spiritual union, has the sanction of Scripture throughout; nay, the spiritual union was the original fact in the mind of God, of which marriage is the transcript (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jr 3:1</reference>, &c.; Eze 16:1-63; 23:1-49; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">Mt 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">25:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="John.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.23-Eph.5.32">Ep 5:23-32</reference>, where Paul does not go from the marriage relation to the union of Christ and the Church as if the former were the first; but comes down from the latter as the first and best recognized fact on which the relation of marriage is based; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">22:17</reference>). Above all, the Song seems to correspond to, and form a trilogy with, Psalms 45 and 72, which contain the same imagery; just as Psalm 37 answers to Proverbs, and the Psalms 39 and 73 to Job. Love to Christ is the strongest, as it is the purest, of human passions, and therefore needs the strongest language to express it: to the pure in heart the phraseology, drawn from the rich imagery of Oriental poetry, will not only appear not indelicate or exaggerated, but even below the reality. A single emblem is a type; the actual rites, incidents, and persons of the Old Testament were appointed types of truths afterwards to be revealed. But the allegory is a continued metaphor, in which the circumstances are palpably often purely imagery, while the thing signified is altogether real. The clue to the meaning of the Song is not to be looked for in the allegory itself, but in other parts of Scripture. "It lies in the casket of revelation an exquisite gem, engraved with emblematical characters, with nothing literal thereon to break the consistency of their beauty" [Burrowes]. This accounts for the name of God not occurring in it. Whereas in the parable the writer narrates, in the allegory he never does so. The Song throughout consists of immediate addresses either of Christ to the soul, or of the soul to Christ. "The experimental knowledge of Christ's loveliness and the believer's love is the best commentary on the whole of this allegorical Song" [Leighton]. Like the curiously wrought Oriental lamps, which do not reveal the beauty of their transparent emblems until lighted up within, so the types and allegories of Scripture, "the lantern to our path" [Psa 119:105], need the inner light of the Holy Spirit of Jesus to reveal their significance. The details of the allegory are not to be too minutely pressed. In the Song, with an Oriental profusion of imagery, numbers of lovely, sensible objects are aggregated not strictly congruous, but portraying jointly by their very diversity the thousand various and seemingly opposite beauties which meet together in Christ.<div eID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12827" type="x-p"/> The unity of subject throughout, and the recurrence of the same expressions (<reference osisRef="Song.2.6">So 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.3">8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.4">4</reference>; 2:16; 6:3; 7:10; 3:6; 6:10; 8:5), prove the unity of the poem, in opposition to those who make it consist of a number of separate erotic songs. The sudden transitions (for example, from the midnight knocking at a humble cottage to a glorious description of the King) accord with the alternations in the believer's experience. However various the divisions assigned be, most commentators have observed four breaks (whatever more they have imagined), followed by four abrupt beginnings (<reference osisRef="Song.2.7">So 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.4">8:4</reference>). Thus there result five parts, all alike ending in full repose and refreshment. We read (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1Ki 4:32</reference>) that Solomon's songs were "a thousand and five." The odd number five added over the complete thousand makes it not unlikely that the "five" refers to the Song of songs, consisting of five parts.<div eID="gen12827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12828" type="x-p"/> It answers to the idyllic poetry of other nations. The Jews explain it of the union of Jehovah and ancient Israel; the allusions to the temple and the wilderness accord with this; some Christians of Christ and the Church; others of Christ and the individual believer. All these are true; for the Church is one in all ages, the ancient typifying the modern Church, and its history answering to that of each individual soul in it. Jesus "sees all, as if that all were one, loves one, as if that one were all." "The time suited the manner of this revelation; because types and allegories belonged to the old dispensation, which reached its ripeness under Solomon, when the temple was built" [Moody Stuart]. "The daughter of Zion at that time was openly married to Jehovah"; for it is thenceforth that the prophets, in reproving Israel's subsequent sin, speak of it as a breach of her marriage covenant. The songs heretofore sung by her were the preparatory hymns of her childhood; "the last and crowning 'Song of Songs' was prepared for the now mature maiden against the day of her marriage to the King of kings" [Origen]. Solomon was peculiarly fitted to clothe this holy mystery with the lovely natural imagery with which the Song abounds; for "he spake of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon, even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">1Ki 4:33</reference>). A higher qualification was his knowledge of the eternal Wisdom or Word of God (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.1-Prov.8.36">Pr 8:1-36</reference>), the heavenly bridegroom. David, his father, had prepared the way, in Psalms 45 and 72; the son perfected the allegory. It seems to have been written in early life, long before his declension; for after it a song of holy gladness would hardly be appropriate. It was the song of his first love, in the kindness of his youthful espousals to Jehovah.
