Like other inspired books, its sense is not to be restricted to that local and temporary one in which the writer may have understood it; it extends to all ages, and shadows forth everlasting truth (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.20">2Pe 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen12828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> "Oh that I knew how all thy lights combine, and the configurations of their glorie,<div eID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seeing not only how each verse doth shine, but all the constellations of the storie."--</hi>Herbert.<div eID="gen12830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> Three notes of time occur [Moody Stuart]: (1) The Jewish Church speaks of the Gentile Church (<reference osisRef="Song.8.8">So 8:8</reference>) towards the end; (2) Christ speaks to the apostles (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">So 5:1</reference>) in the middle; (3) The Church speaks of the coming of Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">So 1:2</reference>) at the beginning. Thus we have, in direct order, Christ about to come, and the cry for the advent; Christ finishing His work on earth, and the last supper; Christ ascended, and the call of the Gentiles. In another aspect we have: (1) In the individual soul the longing for the manifestation of Christ to it, and the various alternations in its experience (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">So 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>; 2:8; 3:<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.6">1, 4, 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.7">7</reference>) of His manifestation; (2) The abundant enjoyment of His sensible consolations, which is soon withdrawn through the bride's carelessness (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1-Song.5.3">So 5:1-3</reference>, &c.), and her longings after Him, and reconciliation (So 5:8-16; 6:3, &c.; <reference osisRef="Song.7.1">So 7:1</reference>, &c.); (3) Effects of Christ's manifestation on the believer; namely, assurance, labors of love, anxiety for the salvation of the impenitent, eagerness for the Lord's second coming (<reference osisRef="Song.7.10">So 7:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.7.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.8-Song.8.10">8:8-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.8.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Song.1.1-Song.1.17">So 1:1-17</reference>. Canticle I.--(<reference osisRef="Song.1.2-Song.2.7">So 1:2-2:7</reference>)--The Bride Searching for and Finding the King.</title> <div sID="gen12832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8192"/><hi type="bold">1. The song of songs--</hi>The most excellent of all songs, Hebrew idiom (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Ex 29:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.14">De 10:14</reference>). A foretaste on earth of the "new song" to be sung in glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Re 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.3">14:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2-Rev.15.4">15:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen12832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Solomon's--</hi>"King of Israel," or "Jerusalem," is not added, as in the opening of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, not because Solomon had not yet ascended the throne [Moody Stuart], but because his personality is hid under that of Christ, the true Solomon (equivalent to Prince of Peace). The earthly Solomon is not introduced, which would break the consistency of the allegory. Though the bride bears the chief part, the Song throughout is not hers, but that of her "Solomon." He animates her. He and she, the Head and the members, form but one Christ [Adelaide Newton]. Aaron prefigured Him as priest; Moses, as prophet; David, as a suffering king; Solomon, as the triumphant prince of peace. The camp in the wilderness represents the Church in the world; the peaceful reign of Solomon, after all enemies had been subdued, represents the Church in heaven, of which joy the Song gives a foretaste. <div eID="gen12833" type="x-p"/>
entries.47e82a88e0e350e1a28b70793c559c2da2766302: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8193"/><div sID="gen12834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8193"/><hi type="bold">2. him--</hi>abruptly. She names him not, as is natural to one whose heart is full of some much desired friend: so Mary Magdalene at the sepulchre (<reference osisRef="John.20.15">Joh 20:15</reference>), as if everyone must know whom she means, the one chief object of her desire (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.25">Psa 73:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44-Matt.13.46">Mt 13:44-46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.7">Php 3:7</reference>,<reference osisRef="Phil.3.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen12834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kiss--</hi>the token of peace from the Prince of Peace (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.20">Lu 15:20</reference>); "our Peace" (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.10">Psa 85:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.21">Col 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of his mouth--</hi>marking the tenderest affection. For a king to permit his hands, or even garment, to be kissed, was counted a great honor; but that he should himself kiss another with his mouth is the greatest honor. God had in times past spoken by the mouth of His prophets, who had declared the Church's betrothal; the bride now longs for contact with the mouth of the Bridegroom Himself (<reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Lu 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">He 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>). True of the Church before the first advent, longing for "the hope of Israel," "the desire of all nations"; also the awakened soul longing for the kiss of reconciliation; and further, the kiss that is the token of the marriage contract (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Ho 2:19</reference>, 20), and of friendship (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1Sa 20:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.21">Joh 14:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.15">15:15</reference>).<div eID="gen12836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy love--</hi>Hebrew, "loves," namely, tokens of love, loving blandishments.<div eID="gen12837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wine--</hi>which makes glad "the heavy heart" of one ready to perish, so that he "remembers his misery no more" (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Pr 31:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.7">7</reference>). So, in a "better" sense, Christ's love (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.17">Ha 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.18">18</reference>). He gives the same praise to the bride's love, with the emphatic addition, "How much" (<reference osisRef="Song.4.10">So 4:10</reference>). Wine was created by His first miracle (<reference osisRef="John.2.1-John.2.11">Joh 2:1-11</reference>), and was the pledge given of His love at the last supper. The spiritual wine is His blood and His spirit, the "new" and better wine of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.29">Mt 26:29</reference>), which we can never drink to "excess," as the other (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.18">Ep 5:18</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12838" type="x-p"/>
entries.052ef854e5c1f39beabcf55b8912cf1b67a15032: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8194"/><div sID="gen12839" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8194"/>3. Rather, "As regards the savor of thy ointments, it is good" [Maurer]. In <reference osisRef="Song.4.10">So 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">11</reference>, the Bridegroom reciprocates the praise of the bride in the same terms.<div eID="gen12839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12840" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy name--</hi>Christ's character and office as the "Anointed" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">61:1</reference>), as "the savor of ointments" are the graces that surround His person (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">8</reference>). <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Ec 7:1</reference>, in its fullest sense, applies to Him. The holy anointing oil of the high priest, which it was death for anyone else to make (so <reference osisRef="Acts.4.12">Ac 4:12</reference>), implies the exclusive preciousness of Messiah's name (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23-Exod.28.31">Ex 30:23-28, 31</reference>-<reference osisRef="Exod.28.38">38</reference>). So Mary brake the box of precious ointment over Him, appropriately (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.5">Mr 14:5</reference>), the broken box typifying His body, which, when broken, diffused all grace: compounded of various spices, &c. (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>; 2:9); of sweet odor (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.2">Ep 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poured--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Is 53:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>because of the manifestation of God's character in Christ (<reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.19">19</reference>). So the penitent woman (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.37">Lu 7:37</reference>, 38, 47).<div eID="gen12842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgins--</hi>the pure in heart (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Co 11:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>). The same Hebrew is translated, "thy hidden ones" (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Psa 83:3</reference>). The "ointment" of the Spirit "poured forth" produces the "love of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Ro 5:5</reference>). <div eID="gen12843" type="x-p"/>
entries.e52f7c349e8397919f9301de2f1dae3091a517fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8195"/><div sID="gen12844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8195"/>4. (1) The cry of ancient Israel for Messiah, for example, Simeon, Anna, &c. (2) The cry of an awakened soul for the drawing of the Spirit, after it has got a glimpse of Christ's loveliness and its own helplessness.<div eID="gen12844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Draw me--</hi>The Father draws (<reference osisRef="John.6.44">Joh 6:44</reference>). The Son draws (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Ho 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.32">Joh 12:32</reference>). "Draw" here, and "Tell" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.7">So 1:7</reference>), reverently qualify the word "kiss" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">So 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12846" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me, we--</hi>No believer desires to go to heaven alone. We are converted as individuals; we follow Christ as joined in a communion of saints (<reference osisRef="John.1.41">Joh 1:41</reference>, 45). Individuality and community meet in the bride.<div eID="gen12846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">run--</hi>Her earnestness kindles as she prays (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Psa 119:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.60">60</reference>).<div eID="gen12847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after thee--</hi>not before (<reference osisRef="John.10.4">Joh 10:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king ... brought me into--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">Psa 45:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.16">Joh 10:16</reference>). He is the anointed Priest (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>); King (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chambers--</hi>Her prayer is answered even beyond her desires. Not only is she permitted to run after Him, but is brought into the inmost pavilion, where Eastern kings admitted none but the most intimate friends (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.11">Es 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.5.2">5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>). The erection of the temple of Solomon was the first bringing of the bride into permanent, instead of migratory, chambers of the King. Christ's body on earth was the next (<reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>), whereby believers are brought within the veil (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">He 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.20">20</reference>). Entrance into the closet for prayer is the first step. The earnest of the future bringing into heaven (<reference osisRef="John.14.3">Joh 14:3</reference>). His chambers are the bride's also (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>). There are various chambers, plural (<reference osisRef="John.14.2">Joh 14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be glad and rejoice--</hi>inward and outward rejoicing.<div eID="gen12851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">Php 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.4">4</reference>). Not in our spiritual frames (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Psa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen12852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember--</hi>rather, "commemorate with praises" (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Is 63:7</reference>). The mere remembrance of spiritual joys is better than the present enjoyment of carnal ones (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen12853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upright--</hi>rather, "uprightly," "sincerely" (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.1">Psa 58:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.9">Ro 12:9</reference>); so Nathanael (<reference osisRef="John.1.47">Joh 1:47</reference>); Peter (<reference osisRef="John.21.17">Joh 21:17</reference>); or "deservedly" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen12854" type="x-p"/>
entries.08eef17cf3264be1bcb50b0d4c5985415caa3d50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8196"/><div sID="gen12855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8196"/><hi type="bold">5. black--</hi>namely, "as the tents of Kedar," equivalent to blackness (<reference osisRef="Ps.120.5">Psa 120:5</reference>). She draws the image from the black goatskins with which the Scenite Arabs ("Kedar" was in Arabia-Petræa) cover their tents (contrasted with the splendid state tent in which the King was awaiting His bride according to Eastern custom); typifying the darkness of man's natural state. To feel this, and yet also feel one's self in Jesus Christ "comely as the curtains of Solomon," marks the believer (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.18">Ro 7:18</reference>, &c.; 8:1); <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>, "I am chief"; so she says not merely, "I was," but "I am"; still black in herself, but comely through His comeliness put upon her (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Eze 16:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curtains--</hi>first, the hangings and veil in the temple of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.10">Eze 16:10</reference>); then, also, the "fine linen which is the righteousness of saints" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>), the white wedding garment provided by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.11">Mt 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>; 2:10; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.14">Re 7:14</reference>). Historically, the dark tents of Kedar represent the Gentile Church (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.3-Isa.60.7">Is 60:3-7</reference>, &c.). As the vineyard at the close is transferred from the Jews, who had not kept their own, to the Gentiles, so the Gentiles are introduced at the commencement of the Song; for they were among the earliest enquirers after Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.1-Matt.2.12">Mt 2:1-12</reference>): the wise men from the East (Arabia, or Kedar).<div eID="gen12856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Jerusalem--</hi>professors, not the bride, or "the virgins," yet not enemies; invited to gospel blessings (<reference osisRef="Song.3.10">So 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">11</reference>); so near to Jesus Christ as not to be unlikely to find Him (<reference osisRef="Song.5.8">So 5:8</reference>); desirous to seek Him with her (<reference osisRef="Song.6.1">So 6:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Song.6.13">So 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.7.1">7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.5.8">5, 8</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Song.7.8">So 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.7.9">9</reference>, the bride's Beloved becomes their Beloved; not, however, of all of them (<reference osisRef="Song.8.4">So 8:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.23.27">Lu 23:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.28">28</reference>). <div eID="gen12857" type="x-p"/>
entries.c175b53f39469816da0de37ef9ddb67abbbc2a86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8197"/><div sID="gen12858" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8197"/>6. She feels as if her blackness was so great as to be gazed at by all.<div eID="gen12858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mother's children--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.10.36">Mt 10:36</reference>). She is to forget "her own people and her father's house," that is, the worldly connections of her unregenerate state (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.10">Psa 45:10</reference>); they had maltreated her (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.15">Lu 15:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.16">16</reference>). Children of the same mother, but not the same father [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="John.8.41-John.8.44">Joh 8:41-44</reference>). They made her a common keeper of vineyards, whereby the sun looked upon, that is, burnt her; thus she did "not keep her own" vineyard, that is, fair beauty. So the world, and the soul (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.25">Lu 9:25</reference>). The believer has to watch against the same danger (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">1Co 9:27</reference>). So he will be able, instead of the self-reproach here, to say as in <reference osisRef="Song.8.12">So 8:12</reference>. <div eID="gen12859" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf69655465df055e42b47a5738c54f1d3a500b62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8198"/><div sID="gen12860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8198"/><hi type="bold">7. my soul loveth--</hi>more intense than "the virgins" and "the upright love thee" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.37">Mt 22:37</reference>). To carry out the design of the allegory, the royal encampment is here represented as moving from place to place, in search of green pastures, under the Shepherd King (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference>). The bride, having first enjoyed communion with him in the pavilion, is willing to follow Him into labors and dangers; arising from all absorbing love (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Lu 14:26</reference>); this distinguishes her from the formalist (<reference osisRef="John.10.27">Joh 10:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Re 14:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feedest--</hi>tendest thy flock (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Is 40:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.20">He 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.25">1Pe 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.4">5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.17">Re 7:17</reference>). No single type expresses all the office of Jesus Christ; hence arises the variety of diverse images used to portray the manifold aspects of Him: these would be quite incongruous, if the Song referred to the earthly Solomon. Her intercourse with Him is peculiar. She hears His voice, and addresses none but Himself. Yet it is through a veil; she sees Him not (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8">Job 23:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">9</reference>). If we would be fed, we must follow the Shepherd through the whole breadth of His Word, and not stay on one spot alone.<div eID="gen12861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">makest ... to rest--</hi>distinct from "feedest"; periods of rest are vouchsafed after labor (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.10">49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13-Ezek.34.15">Eze 34:13-15</reference>). Communion in private must go along with public following of Him.<div eID="gen12862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turneth aside--</hi>rather one veiled, that is, as a harlot, not His true bride (<reference osisRef="Gen.38.15">Ge 38:15</reference>), [Gesenius]; or as a mourner (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>), [Weiss]; or as one unknown [Maurer]. All imply estrangement from the Bridegroom. She feels estranged even among Christ's true servants, answering to "thy companions" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.28">Lu 22:28</reference>), so long as she has not Himself present. The opposite spirit to <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">1Co 3:4</reference>. <div eID="gen12863" type="x-p"/>
entries.5864d12b2e387fd7b6fcbf3795d46f1a2ff479f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8199"/><div sID="gen12864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8199"/><hi type="bold">8. If--</hi>she ought to have known (<reference osisRef="John.14.8">Joh 14:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.9">9</reference>). The confession of her ignorance and blackness (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>) leads Him to call her "fairest" (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.20">Mt 12:20</reference>). Her jealousy of letting even "His companions" take the place of Himself (<reference osisRef="Song.1.7">So 1:7</reference>) led her too far. He directs her to follow them, as they follow Him (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1Co 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">He 6:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.12">12</reference>); to use ordinances and the ministry; where they are, He is (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jr 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.18.19">Mt 18:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>). Indulging in isolation is not the way to find Him. It was thus, literally, that Zipporah found her bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.16">Ex 2:16</reference>). The bride unhesitatingly asks the watchmen afterwards (<reference osisRef="Song.3.3">So 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen12864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kids--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.21.15">Joh 21:15</reference>). Christ is to be found in active ministrations, as well as in prayer (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.25">Pr 11:25</reference>).<div eID="gen12865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shepherds' tents--</hi>ministers in the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.1">Psa 84:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12866" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd14b33a40eb918ba33a7e3276d4eb29c3faa05e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8200"/><div sID="gen12867" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8200"/><hi type="bold">9. horses in Pharaoh's chariots--</hi>celebrated for beauty, swiftness, and ardor, at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.15">Ex 14:15</reference>). These qualities, which seem to belong to the ungodly, really belong to the saints [Moody Stuart]. The allusion may be to the horses brought at a high price by Solomon out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Chr.1.16">2Ch 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>). So the bride is redeemed out of spiritual Egypt by the true Solomon, at an infinite price (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Is 51:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>). But the deliverance from Pharaoh at the Red Sea accords with the allusion to the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.7">7</reference>); it rightly is put at the beginning of the Church's call. The ardor and beauty of the bride are the point of comparison; (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>) "run"; (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>) "comely." Also, like Pharaoh's horses, she forms a great company (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.14">14</reference>). As Jesus Christ is both Shepherd and Conqueror, so believers are not only His sheep, but also, as a Church militant now, His chariots and horses (<reference osisRef="Song.6.4">So 6:4</reference>). <div eID="gen12867" type="x-p"/>
entries.55d50c49295ac5938f5439113fbf45fefbd4bdda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8201"/><div sID="gen12868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8201"/><hi type="bold">10. rows of jewels--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.11-Ezek.16.13">Eze 16:11-13</reference>). Olerius says, Persian ladies wear two or three rows of pearls round the head, beginning on the forehead and descending down to the cheeks and under the chin, so that their faces seem to be set in pearls (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.11">Eze 16:11</reference>). The comparison of the horses (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>) implies the vital energy of the bride; this verse, her superadded graces (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pr 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Ti 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.5">2Pe 1:5</reference>). <div eID="gen12868" type="x-p"/>
entries.79f4246b973449dce6eed9b2870ffed0dcd60db4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8202"/><div sID="gen12869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8202"/><hi type="bold">11. We--</hi>the Trinity implied by the Holy Ghost, whether it was so by the writer of the Song or not (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.26">Ge 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Pr 8:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">30:4</reference>). "The Jews acknowledged God as king, and Messiah as king, in interpreting the Song, but did not know that these two are one" [Leighton].<div eID="gen12869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make--</hi>not merely give (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">borders of gold, with studs of silver--</hi>that is, "spots of silver"--Jesus Christ delights to give more "to him that hath" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.29">Mt 25:29</reference>). He crowns His own work in us (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.12">Is 26:12</reference>). The "borders" here are equivalent to "rows" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.10">So 1:10</reference>); but here, the King seems to give the finish to her attire, by adding a crown (borders, or circles) of gold studded with silver spots, as in <reference osisRef="Esth.2.17">Es 2:17</reference>. Both the royal and nuptial crown, or chaplet. The Hebrew for "spouse" (<reference osisRef="Song.4.8">So 4:8</reference>) is a crowned one (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.12">Eze 16:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>). The crown is given at once upon conversion, in title, but in sensible possession afterwards (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen12871" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab79e790752bf2a14ed5871e1b2b5381ea0882a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8203"/><div sID="gen12872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8203"/><hi type="bold">12. While--</hi>It is the presence of the Sun of Righteousness that draws out the believer's odors of grace. It was the sight of Him at table that caused the two women to bring forth their ointments for Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.37">Lu 7:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.38">38</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.3">Joh 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2Co 2:15</reference>). Historically fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.11">Mt 2:11</reference>); spiritually (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Re 3:20</reference>); and in church worship (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.20">Mt 18:20</reference>); and at the Lord's Supper especially, for here public communion with Him at table amidst His friends is spoken of, as <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference> refers to private communion (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.16">1Co 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.21">21</reference>); typically (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.9-Exod.24.11">Ex 24:9-11</reference>); the future perfect fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Lu 22:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">Re 19:9</reference>). The allegory supposes the King to have stopped in His movements and to be seated with His friends on the divan. What grace that a table should be prepared for us, while still militant (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>)!<div eID="gen12872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my spikenard--</hi>not boasting, but owning the Lord's grace to and in her. The spikenard is a lowly herb, the emblem of humility. She rejoices that He is well pleased with her graces, His own work (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">Php 4:18</reference>). <div eID="gen12873" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeb9d4c608288cf1863107b92587e2f98a3595c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8204"/><div sID="gen12874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8204"/><hi type="bold">13. bundle of myrrh--</hi>abundant preciousness (Greek), (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>). Even a little myrrh was costly; much more a bundle (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>). Burrowes takes it of a scent-box filled with liquid myrrh; the liquid obtained by incision gave the tree its chief value.<div eID="gen12874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>rather, "it"; it is the myrrh that lies in the bosom, as the cluster of camphire is in the vineyards (<reference osisRef="Song.1.14">So 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all night--</hi>an undivided heart (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Ep 3:17</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jr 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.15">Eze 16:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.30">30</reference>). Yet on account of the everlasting covenant, God restores the adulteress (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.62">62</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.2">Ho 2:2</reference>, &c.). The night is the whole present dispensation till the everlasting day dawns (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Ro 13:12</reference>). Also, literally, "night" (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.147">Psa 119:147</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.148">148</reference>), the night of affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.8">Psa 42:8</reference>). <div eID="gen12876" type="x-p"/>
entries.82846d9f556a59bea386c686600549db124ea445: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8205"/><div sID="gen12877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8205"/><hi type="bold">14. cluster--</hi>Jesus Christ is one, yet manifold in His graces.<div eID="gen12877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">camphire--</hi>or, "cypress." The "hennah" is meant, whose odorous flowers grow in clusters, of a color white and yellow softly blended; its bark is dark, the foliage light green. Women deck their persons with them. The loveliness of Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen12878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vineyards--</hi>appropriate in respect to Him who is "the vine." The spikenard was for the banquet (<reference osisRef="Song.1.12">So 1:12</reference>); the myrrh was in her bosom continually (<reference osisRef="Song.1.13">So 1:13</reference>); the camphire is in the midst of natural beauties, which, though lovely, are eclipsed by the one cluster, Jesus Christ, pre-eminent above them all.<div eID="gen12879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">En-gedi--</hi>in South Palestine, near the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.62">Jos 15:62</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>), famed for aromatic shrubs. <div eID="gen12880" type="x-p"/>
entries.888881ec12daa1e5aaf532216974fb03eb72d441: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8206"/><div sID="gen12881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8206"/><hi type="bold">15. fair--</hi>He discerns beauty in her, who had said, "I am black" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>), because of the everlasting covenant (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.11">Psa 45:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Is 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>,<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen12881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doves' eyes--</hi>large and beautiful in the doves of Syria. The prominent features of her beauty (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>), gentleness, innocence, and constant love, emblem of the Holy Ghost, who changes us to His own likeness (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.10">Ge 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Mt 3:16</reference>). The opposite kind of eyes (<reference osisRef="Ps.101.5">Psa 101:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.20.15">Mt 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2Pe 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen12882" type="x-p"/>
entries.54e15562282a8e6777f85b1fa10a7be3d9982f98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8207"/><div sID="gen12883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8207"/>16. Reply of the Bride. She presumes to call Him beloved, because He called her so first. Thou callest me "fair"; if I am so, it is not in myself; it is all from Thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">Psa 90:17</reference>); but Thou art fair in Thyself (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">Psa 45:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.3.17">Pr 3:17</reference>) towards Thy friends (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.26">2Sa 1:26</reference>).<div eID="gen12884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bed ... green--</hi>the couch of green grass on which the King and His bride sit to "rest at noon." Thus her prayer in <reference osisRef="Song.1.7">So 1:7</reference> is here granted; a green oasis in the desert, always found near waters in the East (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.17-Isa.41.19">Is 41:17-19</reference>). The scene is a kiosk, or summer house. Historically, the literal resting of the Babe of Beth-lehem and his parents on the green grass provided for cattle (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.7">Lu 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). In this verse there is an incidental allusion, in <reference osisRef="Song.1.15">So 1:15</reference>, to the offering (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.24">Lu 2:24</reference>). So the "cedar and fir" ceiling refers to the temple (1Ki 5:6-10; 6:<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.15-1Kgs.10.18">15-18</reference>); type of the heavenly temple (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Re 21:22</reference>). <div eID="gen12885" type="x-p"/>
entries.0329ca5795102681c850f7ff7154e1e2a45255d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8208"/><div sID="gen12886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8208"/><hi type="bold">17. our house--</hi>see on <reference osisRef="Song.1.16">So 1:16</reference>; but primarily, the kiosk (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Is 11:10</reference>), "His rest." Cedar is pleasing to the eye and smell, hard, and never eaten by worms.<div eID="gen12886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fir--</hi>rather, "cypress," which is hard, durable, and fragrant, of a reddish hue [Gesenius, Weiss, and Maurer]. Contrasted with the shifting "tents" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.5">So 1:5</reference>), His house is "our house" (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">Psa 92:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Ep 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">He 3:6</reference>). Perfect oneness of Him and the bride (<reference osisRef="John.14.20">Joh 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.21">17:21</reference>). There is the shelter of a princely roof from the sun (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.6">Psa 121:6</reference>), without the confinement of walls, and amidst rural beauties. The carved ceiling represents the wondrous excellencies of His divine nature. <chapter eID="Song.1"/>

entries.ed29d048bbe59e6b00065791e2f12b7b0e48f72f: <div eID="gen25810" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Canticles,or Song of Solomon</title> <div sID="gen25811" type="x-p"/> The book before us is called in the Hebrew שיר השירים Shir Hashshirim, "The Song of Songs;" or, "An Ode of the Odes:" which might be understood, "An Ode taken or selected from others of a similar kind;" or, "An Ode the most excellent of all others;" this being an idiom common to the Hebrew language: e.g., the God of gods is the supreme God; the Lord of lords, the supreme Lord; the King of kings, the supreme King; the heaven of heavens, the supreme or highest heaven. It may therefore be designed to express "a song of the utmost perfection; one of the best that existed, or had ever been penned." Perhaps the title may have a reference to the other poetical compositions of Solomon, which were no less than one thousand and five; and this was considered the most excellent of the whole, and the only one that remains, unless we suppose Solomon, with some of the Jews, to be the author of Psalms 72 and <reference osisRef="Psa.127.1-Psa.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference> : but this cannot be proved. <div eID="gen25811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25812" type="x-p"/> There have been some doubts concerning the author of this book. Some of the rabbins supposed it to be the work of the prophet Isaiah; but this sentiment never gained much credit. Most have, without hesitation, attributed it to Solomon, whose name it bears; and if the book of Ecclesiastes be his, this will follow in course, as the style is exactly the same, allowing for the difference of the subject. Both books seem to have been written about the same time, and to have had the same author. <div eID="gen25812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25813" type="x-p"/> This book, if written by Solomon, could not have been written in his old age, as some have supposed the book of Ecclesiastes to have been; which sentiment is, I think, sufficiently disproved; for we find that long before Solomon's old age he had three hundred wives, and seven hundred concubines; but at the time this Song was written, Solomon had only sixty wives and eighty concubines. And the Song most certainly celebrates a marriage; whether between Solomon and the daughter of Pharaoh, or between him and some Jewish princess, has not been fully agreed on among critics and commentators. It is most likely to have been a juvenile or comparatively juvenile production; and indeed the high and glowing colouring, and the strength of the images, are full proofs of this. Though Anacreon made amatory odes when he was bald-headed, yet neither he nor any one else, humanly speaking, could have made such odes as the Canticles when stricken in years. <div eID="gen25813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25814" type="x-p"/> But to what denomination of writing do the Canticles belong? Are they mere Odes, or Idyls, or Pastorals; or are they an Epithalamium? Let us define these terms, and examine the Song of Solomon by them. <div eID="gen25814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25815" type="x-p"/> 1. The Ode is generally understood to be a species of poetry containing sublime and important matter, always sung, or accompanied by the harp, or some proper musical instrument. <div eID="gen25815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25816" type="x-p"/> 2. The Idyl implies a short poem, containing some adventure. <div eID="gen25816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25817" type="x-p"/> 3. The Pastoral contains what belongs to shepherds, and their occupations. <div eID="gen25817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25818" type="x-p"/> 4. The Epithalamium is the congratulatory song, sung to a new married pair, wishing them abundant blessings, a numerous and happy offspring, etc. <div eID="gen25818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25819" type="x-p"/> Strictly speaking, the Book of Canticles falls under neither of these descriptions: it is rather a composition sui generis, and seems to partake more of the nature of what we call a Mask, than any thing else; an entertainment for the guests who attended the marriage ceremony, with a dramatic cast throughout the whole, though the persons who speak and act are not formally introduced. There are so many touches in the form and manner of this Song like those in the Comus of Milton, that it leads me to doubt whether the English poet has not taken the idea of his mask from the Jewish. <div eID="gen25819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25820" type="x-p"/> As to the persons, chiefly concerned, it is generally believed that Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter are the bridegroom and bride; with their proper attendants, viz., companions of the bridegroom, and companions of the bride, with certain mutes, who only appear, or are mentioned by others, without taking any particular part in the transactions. <div eID="gen25820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25821" type="x-p"/> But it is much more easy to be satisfied on the species of composition to which this book belongs, than on the meaning of the book itself. Is it to be understood in the obvious manner in which it presents itself? And are Solomon and his bride, their friends and companions, to be considered as mere dramatis personae? Or are they typical or representative persons? Does this marriage represent a celestial union? Do the speeches of each contain Divine doctrines? Are the metaphors, taken from earthly things, to be understood of spiritual matters? In a word, does Solomon here represent Jesus Christ. Is the daughter of Pharaoh the Christian Church; or, according to some Roman Catholics, the Virgin Mary? Are watchmen, vineyard-keepers, shepherds, etc., the ministers of the Gospel? Wine and vartous fruits, the influences and graces of the Divine Spirit? etc., etc. How multitudinous and positive are the affirmative answers to these questions! And yet, though the many agree in the general principle, how various their expositions of the different parts of the piece! And where, all this time, is the proof that the principle is not misunderstood? As to conjectures, they are as uncertain as they are endless; and what one pious or learned man may think to be the meaning, is no proof to any other that he should make up his mind in the same way. <div eID="gen25821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25822" type="x-p"/> Let us for a moment consider the different opinions held on this book, without entering into the discussion of their propriety or impropriety. They are the following: - <div eID="gen25822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25823" type="x-p"/> I. It is a plain epithalamium on the marriage of Solomon with the daughter of Pharaoh, king of Egypt; and is to be understood in no other way. <div eID="gen25823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25824" type="x-p"/> II. It is an allegory relative to the conduct of God towards the Hebrews, in bringing them out of Egypt, through the wilderness to the Promised Land. <div eID="gen25824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25825" type="x-p"/> III. It is intended to represent the incarnation of Jesus Christ, or his marriage with human nature, in reference to its redemption. <div eID="gen25825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25826" type="x-p"/> IV. It represents Christ's love to the Church or elected souls, and their love to him. <div eID="gen25826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25827" type="x-p"/> V. It is an allegorical poem on the glories of Jesus Christ and the Virgin Mary. <div eID="gen25827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25828" type="x-p"/> VI. It is a collection of sacred idyls; the spiritual meaning of which is not agreed on. <div eID="gen25828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25829" type="x-p"/> Now each of these opinions has its powerful supporters, and each of these has reasons to offer for the support of the opinion which is espoused; and nothing but a direct revelation from God can show us which of these opinions is the correct one, or whether any of them are correct. <div eID="gen25829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25830" type="x-p"/> The antiquity of an opinion, if that be not founded on a revelation from God, is no evidence of its truth; for there are many ungodly opinions which are more than a thousand years old. And as to great men and great names, we find them enrolled and arranged on each side of all controversies. It may be asked, What do Christ and his apostles say of it? <div eID="gen25830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25831" type="x-p"/> 1. If Jesus Christ or any of his apostles had referred to it as an allegory, and told us the subject which it pointed out, the matter would have been plain: we should then have had data, and had only to proceed in the way of elucidation. But we find nothing of this in the New Testament. <div eID="gen25831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25832" type="x-p"/> 2. If they had referred to it as an allegory, without intimating the meaning, then we should be justified in searching everywhere for that meaning; and conjecture itself would have been legal, till we had arrived at some self-testifying issue. <div eID="gen25832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25833" type="x-p"/> 3. If they had referred to it at all, in connection with spiritual subjects, then we should have at once seen that it was to be spiritually understood; and, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we must have humbly sought for its spiritual interpretation. <div eID="gen25833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25834" type="x-p"/> 4. Had the Supreme Being been introduced, or referred to in any of his essential attributes, or by any of the names which he has been pleased to assume in his revelations to men, we should have then seen that the writer was a spiritual man, and wrote probably in reference to a spiritual end; and, that we should pass by or through his letter, in order to get to the spirit concealed under it. <div eID="gen25834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25835" type="x-p"/> But none of these things appear in this book: the name of God is not found in it; nor is it quoted in the New Testament. As to certain references which its allegorical expositors suppose are made to it, either in the Gospels, Epistles, or Apocalypse, they are not express, and do not, by any thing in or connected with them, appear unequivocally to point out this book. And after all that has been said, I am fully of opinion it is not once referred to in the New Testament. But this is no proof of its not being canonical, as there are other books, on which there is no doubt, that are in the same predicament. But still, if it refer so distinctly to Christ and his Church, as some suppose, it certainly would not have been passed over by both evangelists and apostles without pointed and especial notice; and particularly if it points out the love of Christ to his Church, and the whole economy of God's working in reference to the salvation of the souls of men. <div eID="gen25835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25836" type="x-p"/> From all this it will appear to the intelligent reader, that the spiritual meaning of this book cannot easily be made out: <div eID="gen25836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25837" type="x-p"/> 1. Because we do not know that it is an allegory. <div eID="gen25837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25838" type="x-p"/> 2. If one, the principles on which such allegory is to be explained do nowhere appear. <div eID="gen25838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25839" type="x-p"/> Whom then are we to follow in the interpretation of this very singular book? The Targumist, who applies it to God and the Hebrews, in their journeyings from Egypt to the promised land? Origen, who made it a Christian allegory? Apponius, who spiritualized it? Gregory the Great, who in the main copied them? The good man, who in 1717, at Paris, so illustrated it as "to induce men to devote themselves to Jesus Christ and the Virgin Mary?" Mr. Durham, Mr. Robotham, Mr. Ainsworth, Mr. Romaine, and Dr. Gill, who endeavored to prove that it concerns Christ and the elect? Or Mr. Harmer and others who acknowledge it to be an inimitable composition, and to be understood only of Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter? Or, finally, Dr. Mason Good, who considers it a collection of sacred idyls, the spiritual interpretation of which is not agreed on? <div eID="gen25839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25840" type="x-p"/> I had for a long time hesitated whether I should say any thing on this book; not because I did not think I understood its chief design and general meaning, for of this I really have no doubt, but because I did not understand it as a spiritual allegory, representing the loves off Christ and his Church. I must own I see no indubitable ground for this opinion. And is it of no moment whether the doctrines drawn from it, by those who allegorize and spiritualize it, be indubitably founded on it or not? The doctrines may be true in themselves, (which is indeed more than can be said of those of most of its interpreters), but is it not a very solemn, and indeed awful thing to say, This is the voice of Christ to his Church, This is the voice of the Church to Christ, etc., etc., when there is no proof from God, nor from any other portion of his word, that these things are so? <div eID="gen25840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25841" type="x-p"/> It is much better, therefore, if explained or illustrated at all, to take it in its literal meaning, and explain it in its general sense. I say general sense, because there are many passages in it which should not be explained, if taken literally, the references being too delicate; and Eastern phraseology on such subjects is too vivid for European imaginations. Let any sensible and pious medical man read over this book, and, if at all acquainted with Asiatic phraseology, say whether it would be proper, even in medical language, to explain all the descriptions and allusions in this poem. <div eID="gen25841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25842" type="x-p"/> After what I have said on the difficulty of interpreting this book in a spiritual way it would not be fair to withhold from the reader the general arguments on which the theory of its allegorical meaning is founded. The principal part of the commentators on this book, especially those who have made it their separate study, have in general taken it for granted that their mode of interpretation is incontrovertible; and have proceeded to spiritualize every figure and every verse as if they had a Divine warrant for all they have said. Their conduct is dangerous; and the result of their well-intentioned labors has been of very little service to the cause of Christianity in general, or to the interests of true morality in particular. By their mode of interpretation an undignified, not to say mean and carnal, language has been propagated among many well-meaning religious people, that has associated itself too much with selfish and animal affections, and created feelings that accorded little with the dignified spirituality of the religion of the Lord Jesus. I speak not from report; I speak from observation and experience, and observation not hastily made. The conviction on my mind and the conclusion to which I have conscientiously arrived, are the result of frequent examination, careful reading, and close thinking, at intervals, for nearly fifty years; and however I may be blamed by some, and pitied by others, I must say, and I say it as fearlessly as I do conscientiously, that in this inimitably fine elegant Hebrew ode I see nothing of Christ and his Church, and nothing that appears to have been intended to be thus understood; and nothing, if applied in this way, that, per se, can promote the interests of vital godliness, or cause the simple and sincere not to "know Christ after the flesh." Here I conscientiously stand. May God help me! <div eID="gen25842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25843" type="x-p"/> The most rational view of the subject that I have seen is that taken by Mr. Harmer, who has indeed detailed and strengthened the arguments of his predecessors who have declared for the spiritual meaning. In his "Outlines of a Comment upon Solomon's Song," he supposes that the Song refers to Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh; and that he had a Jewish queen, who is frequently referred to in the work; and that, unless this be allowed, there are several important passages in the book that cannot be understood; and indeed it is on this principle that he finds his chief ground for a spiritual and allegorical interpretation. "Whatever was the intention of God," says he, "in bringing about this marriage, and in causing it to be celebrated in such an extraordinary manner, by songs that were directed to be placed among the sacred writings, it is certain there never was any resemblance more striking between the circumstances and transactions of any of the remarkable personages of the Old Testament and those of Messiah, than the likeness we may observe between Solomon marrying a Gentile princess, and making her equal in honor and privileges with his former Jewish queen, and in her being frequently mentioned afterwards in history, while the other is passed over in total silence, and the conduct of the Messiah towards the Gentile and Jewish Churches. "The two remarkable things in the conduct of the Messiah towards the two Churches are the making the Gentiles fellow heirs of the same body and partakers of the promises, without and difference; and the giving up to neglect the Jewish Church, while that of the Gentiles has long flourished in great honor, and been the subject of many a history. St. Paul takes notice of both these circumstances with particular solemnity; of the first, in the third chapter of Ephesians, and elsewhere; of the other, in the eleventh chapter of Romans. They are points, then, that deserve great attention. "They are both called mysteries, (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Rom 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.3">Eph 3:3</reference>), that is, things that had been concealed aforetime; but it by no means follows that there were no shadowy representations of these events in the preceding ages, only that they were not clearly and expressly revealed. "Kingdoms and cities are frequently spoken of in holy writ as women. Sacred as well as secular bodies of men are represented under that image. The universal Church is spoken of under the notion of a bride, and the Messiah as her husband, Ephesians 5: The two Churches of Jews and Gentiles, or the Church under the Mosaic dispensation and the Church freed from those ceremonies, are represented as two women - the one formerly treated as the principal wife; and the second, as having been for a long time neglected, but afterwards producing a much more numerous issue than the first-by the prophet Isaiah in his fifty-fourth chapter, according to the explanation St. Paul has given of that passage in Galatians 4: Particular Churches are mentioned after the same manner. So, concerning the Church at Corinth, St. Paul says, "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ;" <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2Cor 11:2</reference>. "Since then it is common for the Scriptures to represent the Church of God under the notion of a woman, and the Messiah under that of a husband; since the two bodies of men - that which worshipped God according to the Mosaic rites, and that which observed them not - are compared to two women; and since the circumstances of these two Churches are such as I have given an account of from St. Paul, it must be acknowledged that there is a lively resemblance between Solomon's espousing the Egyptian princess and the Messiah's admitting the Gentiles to equal privileges with the Jews, whether it was or was not designed by God as an emblem and type of it celebrated by his prophets for this cause, in holy songs; and those songs preserved with care to this day among writings of the most sacred kind on that account." <div eID="gen25843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25844" type="x-p"/> This is the whole of Mr. Harmer's argument; see his Outlines, pages 74-77. And what is proved by it? Nothing, in reference to this book. We know that the Jewish people, not the Church exclusively, are represented under the notion of a woman addicted, and a wife unfaithful, divorced, and forsaken, etc.; and that the Corinthians were represented under the notion of a chaste virgin espoused to Christ. And we know that all this was done to show, that as the marriage union was the closest, strictest, and most sacred among men, the union of the soul to God, and its connection with him, might be most fitly represented by that union, and unfaithfulness to him by infidelity in the other case. But what has this to do with the Song of Solomon? Where is the intimation that Solomon represents Christ; Pharaoh's daughter, the Church of the Gentiles; and the Jewish queen, the Church of the Israelites? Nowhere. Why then assume the thing that should be proved; and then build doctrines on it, and draw inferences from it, as if the assumption had been demonstrated? <div eID="gen25844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25845" type="x-p"/> Were this mode of interpretation to be applied to the Scriptures in general, (and why not, if legitimate here?) in what a state would religion soon be! Who could see any thing certain, determinate, and fixed in the meaning of the Divine oracles, when fancy and imagination must be the standard interpreters? God has not left his word to man's will in this way. <div eID="gen25845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25846" type="x-p"/> Every attempt, however well-intentioned, to revive this thriftless, not to say dangerous, Origenian method of seducing the Scriptures to particular creeds and purposes, should be regarded with jealousy; and nothing received as the doctrine of the Lord but what may be derived from those plain words of the Most High which lie most on a level with the capacities of mankind. Allegory, metaphor, and figures in general, where the design is clearly indicated, which is the case with all those employed by the sacred writers, may come in to illustrate and more forcibly to apply Divine truth; but to extort celestial meanings from a whole book, where no such indication is given, is most certainly not the way to arrive at the knowledge of the true God, and of Jesus Christ whom he has sent. <div eID="gen25846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25847" type="x-p"/> As the Jewish marriages were celebrated for seven days, it has been often observed that this Song divides itself into seven periods, and describes the transactions of each. <div eID="gen25847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25848" type="x-p"/> I. The First chapter represents the bridegroom and bride as a shepherd and shepherdess. The bride asks her spouse where he takes his flock at noon, to preserve them from the excessive heat, lest she, in seeking him, should go astray into some strange pastures. After this day, the first night succeeds, which is pointed out <reference osisRef="Sol.2.4-Sol.2.6">Sol 2:4-6</reference>. The bridegroom rises early in the morning, leaves the bride asleep, and goes hastily to the fields to his necessary occupations, <reference osisRef="Sol.2.7">Sol 2:7</reference>. <div eID="gen25848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25849" type="x-p"/> II. The Second night is pointed out <reference osisRef="Sol.2.8">Sol 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Sol.2.9">Sol 2:9</reference>, etc. The bridegroom comes to the window of his spouse. She opens it, and he enters; and on the morrow, he returns to the fields to his flocks, <reference osisRef="Sol.2.17">Sol 2:17</reference>. <div eID="gen25849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25850" type="x-p"/> III. The Third night, the bridegroom having delayed his coming, the bride, being uneasy, arises from her bed, and goes out and inquires of the guards of the city, whether they had seen her beloved. She had not gone far from them till she met with him; she conducts him to her apartment, 3:14. Very early in the morning, he retires to the country, leaving the bride asleep, verse 5. Afterwards she arises, and goes also to the fields, verse 6.The Fourth chapter is an eulogium on the bride's beauty; and seems to be a conversation between the parties in the country. She invites the bridegroom to visit her, <reference osisRef="Sol.5.1">Sol 5:1</reference>. He leaves his friends, with whom he was feasting, and comes to the door of his spouse, <reference osisRef="Sol.5.2">Sol 5:2</reference>. She hesitating to let him in, he withdraws and goes to his garden. The bride follows; but, not knowing whither he had retired, asks the guards of the city, by whom she is maltreated; thence goes to the daughters of Jerusalem, and inquires of them, <reference osisRef="Sol.5.3">Sol 5:3</reference>, etc. At last she meets with him, <reference osisRef="Sol.6.1">Sol 6:1</reference>, etc., and having spent some time with him, returns. <div eID="gen25850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25851" type="x-p"/> IV. <reference osisRef="Sol.6.9">Sol 6:9</reference>, points out the Fourth night of the marriage. <div eID="gen25851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25852" type="x-p"/> V. The Fifth night is pointed out <reference osisRef="Sol.7.1">Sol 7:1</reference>, etc. The bridegroom gives his bride nearly the same praise and commendations which he had received from her in the preceding chapters; and early in the morning they go out together to the fields, <reference osisRef="Sol.7.11-Sol.7.13">Sol 7:11-13</reference>. <div eID="gen25852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25853" type="x-p"/> VI. The Sixth night they pass at a village in the country, at the house of a person who is termed the bride's mother, <reference osisRef="Sol.7.13">Sol 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Sol.8.1-Sol.8.3">Sol 8:1-3</reference>. She invites her spouse thither, and promises to regale him with excellent fruits and choice wine; and early in the morning the bridegroom arises, leaves the bride asleep as formerly, and retires to the country, <reference osisRef="Sol.8.4">Sol 8:4</reference>. <div eID="gen25853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25854" type="x-p"/> VII. The Seventh night is passed in the gardens. From <reference osisRef="Sol.8.5">Sol 8:5</reference>, we have a series of dialogues between the bride and bridegroom. In the morning the bridegroom, having perceived that they were overheard, begs the bride to permit him to retire. She assents, <reference osisRef="Sol.8.13">Sol 8:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Sol.8.14">Sol 8:14</reference>, and exhorts him "to make haste, and be like a roe or a young hart on the mountains of spices." <div eID="gen25854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25855" type="x-p"/> This is the division, which is in the main most followed, especially by the best critics. But, besides this, several others have been proposed; and the reader, who wishes to enter more particularly into the subject, may consult Bishop Bossuet, Calmet, and Bishop Lowth. For my own part I doubt the propriety of this technical arrangement, and do not think that any thing of the kind was intended by the author. The division is not obvious; and therefore, in my apprehension, not natural. Of Dr. Good's division I shall speak below. <div eID="gen25855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25856" type="x-p"/> The dramatis personae have been marked by some of the ancient interpreters, and the different portions of the whole Song appointed to several persons who are specified; and this division served for the basis of a commentary. The most regular division of this kind with which I have met is in a MS. of my own; the Bible which I have often quoted in my comment. <div eID="gen25856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25857" type="x-p"/> This, attributed by some to Wiclif, and by others to an older translator, I have carefully transcribed, with all the distinction of parts and speeches. The translation is very simple; and in many cases is much more faithful to the meaning of the Hebrew text, though in the main taken from the Vulgate, than our own version. It is a great curiosity, and certainly was never before printed; and is a fine specimen of our mother tongue as spoken in these countries in M.CCCLX., which may be about the date of this translation. On the common mode of interpretation I venture to assert that my readers will understand this Song ten times better from this translation and its rubricks, than they have ever done from all the forms in which it has been presented to them, to the present time. For this addition, I anticipate the thanks of every intelligent reader. The indications of the speakers, printed here in black letter, are all rubrick, in the beautiful original. I have added a short glossary on some of the more difficult or obsolete words, which will assist the less experienced reader, under whose notice such remote specimens of his own tongue seldom fall. <div eID="gen25857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25858" type="x-p"/> Between twenty and thirty years ago I received from India a part of the Gitagovinda, or Songs of Jayadeva. This poet, the finest lyric poet of India, flourished before the Christian era; and the poem above, which makes the tenth book of the Bhagavet, was written professedly to celebrate the loves of Chrishna and Radha, or the reciprocal attraction between the Divine goodness and the human soul. The author leaves us in no doubt concerning the design of this little pastoral drama; for in the conclusion he thus speaks: "Whatever is delightful in the modes of music, whatever is Divine in Meditations on Vishnu, whatever is exquisite in the sweet art of love, whatever is graceful in the fine strains of poetry; all that, let the happy and wise learn from the Songs of Jayadeva, whose soul is united with the foot of Narayan." Vishnu and Narayan are epithets of Christina, or the supreme incarnated god of the Hindoos. I found the general phraseology of this work, and its imagery as well as its subject, to correspond so much with those of the Song of Solomon, that in the short notes which I wrote on this book in 1798, I proposed the illustration of many of its passages from the Gitagovinda; and was pleased to find, several years after, that my view of the subject had been confirmed by that encyclopedia of learning and science, Dr. Mason Good, who in his translation of the Song of Songs, with critical notes, published 1803, 8vo., has illustrated many passages from the Gitagovinda. <div eID="gen25858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25859" type="x-p"/> After having made a selection from this ancient poet for the illustration of the Song of Solomon, I changed in some measure my purpose, and determined to give the whole work, and leave it to my readers to apply those passages which they might think best calculated to throw light upon a book which professedly has the wisest of men for its author, and according to the opinion of many, the most important doctrines of the Christian religion for its subject. I have now followed the metrical version which I received from India, but rather the prose translation of Sir William Jones; dividing it into parts and verses, after the model of the metrical version above mentioned; and adding verbal interpretations of the principal proper names and difficult terms which are contained in the work. <div eID="gen25859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25860" type="x-p"/> Having been long convinced that the Chaldee Taryum is at once the oldest and most valuable comment upon this book, I have also added this. And here I might say that I have not only followed my own judgment, but that also of a very learned divine, Dr. John Gill, who, having preached one hundred and twenty-two sermons on the Song of Solomon, to the Baptist congregation at Horsleydown, near London, embodied them all in what he calls "An Exposition" of this book; to which he added a translation of the Targum, with short explanatory notes, folio, 1728. This was, however, suppressed in all the later editions of this exposition; but why, I cannot tell. This piece I give to my readers, and for the same reasons alleged by this very learned and excellent man himself: - "At the end of this exposition I have given," says he, "a version of the Targum or Chaldee paraphrase upon the whole book, with some notes thereon, induced hereunto by the following reasons: "First, to gratify the curiosity of some who, observing frequent mention and use made of it in my exposition, might be desirous of perusing the whole. "Secondly, for the profitableness thereof. Our learned countryman, Mr. Broughton, says, this paraphrase is worth our study both for delight and profit. It expounds several passages of Scripture, and some in the New Testament, which I have directed to in my notes upon it; and I am persuaded that the writings of the Jews, the ancient Jews especially, would give us much light into the phraseology and sense of abundance of texts in the New Testament." <div eID="gen25860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25861" type="x-p"/> It is certain that this paraphrase does very often direct us, or at least confirm us, as to the persons speaking in this Song, to know which is of very great use in the explication of it. I shall add another reason: I believe the Song of Solomon refers more to the Jewish than to the Christian Church, and I think the Targumist has made a more rational use of it than any of his successors. <div eID="gen25861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25862" type="x-p"/> I have thus places within the reach of all my readers Three especial helps towards a good understanding of this book: <div eID="gen25862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25863" type="x-p"/> 1. The ancient English translation, with its curious dramatis personae <div eID="gen25863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25864" type="x-p"/> 2. The Gitagovinda, a most curious poem of the spiritual and allegorical kind. <div eID="gen25864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25865" type="x-p"/> 3. The Chaldee Targam, the oldest comment on this Song. And I add my prayer, May God guide the reader into all truth, through Christ Jesus!
