Heb. calls the gentlest death the death בנשׁיקה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by which God takes away the soul with a kiss.
entries.45038c7874326c4da1e54b968e31905191dc17d4: Sol 1:4 <div eID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12485" type="x-p"/> The second pentastich also begins with a solo: 4 Draw me, so will we run after thee. <div eID="gen12485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> All recent interpreters (except Böttcher) translate, like Luther, “Draw me after thee, so we run.” Thus also the Targ., but doubtfully: <hi type="italic">Trahe nos post te et curremus post viam bonitatis tuae</hi>. But the accentuation which gives <hi type="italic">Tiphcha</hi> to משׁ requires the punctuation to be that adopted by the Peshito and the Vulg., and according to which the passage is construed by the Greeks (except, perhaps, by the Quinta): Draw me, so will we, following thee, run (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Dachselt, <hi type="italic">Biblia Accentuata</hi>, p. 983 s.). In reality, this word needs no complement: of itself it already means, one drawing towards, or to himself; the corresponding (Arab.) masak signifies, <hi type="italic">prehendere prehensumque tenere</hi>; the root is מש, <hi type="italic">palpare</hi>, <hi type="italic">contrectare</hi>. It occurs also elsewhere, in a spiritual connection, as the expression of the gentle drawing of love towards itself (Hos 11:4; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer 31:3</reference>); cf. ἑλκύειν, Joh 6:44; Joh 12:32. If one connects “after thee” with “draw me,” then the expression seems to denote that a certain violence is needed to bring the one who is drawn from her place; but if it is connected with “we will run,” then it defines the desire to run expressed by the cohortative, more nearly than a willing obedience or following. The whole chorus, continuing the solo, confesses that there needs only an indication of his wish, a direction given, to make those who here speak eager followers of him whom they celebrate. <div eID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> In what follows, this interchange of the <hi type="italic">solo</hi> and the <hi type="italic">unisono</hi> is repeated: 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi> If the king has brought me into his chambers,      So will we exult and rejoice in thee.      We will praise thy love more than wine!      Uprightly have they loved thee. <div eID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> The cohortative נרוּצה (we will run) was the a<hi type="italic">podosis imperativi</hi>; the cohortatives here are the <hi type="italic">apodosis perfecti hypothetici</hi>. “Suppose that this has happened,” is oftener expressed by the perf. (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.7">Psa 57:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.29">Pro 22:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference>); “suppose that this happens,” by the fut. (<reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>; Ewald, §357 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). חדרי are the <hi type="italic">interiora domus</hi>; the root word hhādǎr, as the Arab. khadar shows, signifies to draw oneself back, to hide; the hhěděr of the tent is the back part, shut off by a curtain from the front space. Those who are singing are not at present in this innermost chamber. But if the king brings one of them in (הביא, from בּוא, <hi type="italic">introire</hi>, with <hi type="italic">acc. loci</hi>), then - they all say - we will rejoice and be glad in thee. The cohortatives are better translated by the fut. than by the conjunctive (<hi type="italic">exultemus</hi>); they express as frequently not what they then desire to do, but what they then are about to do, from inward impulse, with heart delight. The sequence of ideas, “exult” and “rejoice,” is not a <hi type="italic">climax descendens</hi>, but, as <reference osisRef="Ps.118.24">Psa 118:24</reference>, etc., an advance from the external to the internal, - from jubilation which can be feigned, to joy of heart which gives it truth; for שׂמח - according to its root signification: to be smoothed, unwrinkled, to be glad<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Friedr. Delitzsch’s <hi type="italic">Indo-german.-sem. Studien</hi> (1873), p. 99f.</note>  - means to be of a joyful, bright, complaisant disposition; and גּיל, cogn. חיל, to turn (wind) oneself, to revolve, means conduct betokening delight. The prep. ב in verbs of rejoicing, denotes the object on account of which, and in which, one has joy. Then, if admitted into the closest neighbourhood of the king, they will praise his love more than wine. זכר denotes to fix, viz., in the memory; <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.: to bring to remembrance, frequently in the way of praise, and thus directly equivalent to <hi type="italic">celebrare</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ps. 45:18. The wine represents the gifts of the king, in contradistinction to his person. That in inward love he gives himself to them, excels in their esteem all else he gives. For, as the closing line expresses, “uprightly they love thee,” - viz. they love thee, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, from a right heart, which seeks nothing besides, and nothing with thee; and a right mind, which is pleased with thee, and with nothing but thee. Heiligstedt, Zöckler, and others translate: with right they love thee. But the <hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>. מישׁרים (from מישׁר, for which the sing. מישׁור occurs) is an ethical conception (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference>), and signifies, not: the right of the motive, but: the rightness of the word, thought, and act (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.16">Pro 23:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.2">Psa 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>); thus, not: <hi type="italic">jure</hi>; but: <hi type="italic">recte</hi>, <hi type="italic">sincere</hi>, <hi type="italic">candide</hi>. Hengst., Thrupp, and others, falsely render this word like the lxx, Aquil., Symm., Theod., Targ., Jerome, Venet., and Luther, as subject: rectitudes abstr. for concr. = those who have rectitude, the upright. Hengstenberg’s assertion, that the word never occurs as in adv., is set aside by a glance at <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Psa 75:3</reference>; and, on the other hand, there is no passage in which it is sued as <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concr</hi>. It is here, as elsewhere, an adv. acc. for which the word בּמישׁרים might also be used. <div eID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> The second pentastich closes similarly with the first, which ended with “love thee.” What is there said of this king, that the virgins love him, is here more generalized; for <hi type="italic">diligunt te</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">diligeris</hi> (cf. Sol 8:1, Sol 8:7). With these words the table-song ends. It is erotic, and yet so chaste and delicate, - it is sensuous, and yet so ethical, that here, on the threshold, we are at once surrounded as by a mystical cloudy brightness. But how is it to be explained that Solomon, who says (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">Pro 27:2</reference>), “Let another praise thee, and not thine own mouth,” begins this his Song of Songs with a song in praise of himself? It is explained from this, that here he celebrates an incident belonging to the happy beginning of his reign; and for him so far fallen into the past, although not to be forgotten, that what he was and what he now is are almost as two separate persons.
entries.7aa62214fcd0a282d68231f3de975e380f0d691e: Sol 1:5 <div eID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> After this choral song, Shulamith, who has listened to the singers not without being examined by their inquisitive glances as a strange guest not of equal rank with them, now speaks: 5 Black am I, yet comely, ye daughters of Jerusalem,    As the tents of Kedar, as the hangings of Solomon. <div eID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> From this, that she addresses the ladies of the palace as “daughters of Jerusalem” (Kerı̂ ירושׁלים, <hi type="italic">a du. fractus</hi>; like עפרין for עפרון, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>), it is to be concluded that she, although now in Jerusalem, came from a different place. She is, as will afterwards appear, from Lower Galilee; - and it may be remarked, in the interest of the mystical interpretation, that the church, and particularly her first congregations, according to the prophecy, was also Galilean, for Nazareth and Capernaum are their original seats; - and if Shulamith is a poetico-mystical Mashal or emblem, then she represents the synagogue one day to enter into the fellowship of Solomon - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the son of David, and the daughters of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the congregation already believing on the Messiah. Yet we confine ourselves to the nearest sense, in which Solomon relates a self-experience. Shulamith, the lightly esteemed, cannot boast that she is so ruddy and fair of countenance as they who have just sung how pleasant it is to be beloved by this king; but yet she is not so devoid of beauty as not to venture to love and hope to be loved: “Black am I, yet comely.” These words express humility without abjectness. She calls herself “black,” although she is not so dark and unchangeably black as an “Ethiopian” (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jer 13:23</reference>). The verb שׁחר has the general primary idea of growing dark, and signifies not necessarily soot-blackness (modern Arab. shuhwar, soot), but blackness more or less deep, as שׁחר, the name of the morning twilight, or rather the morning grey, shows; for (Arab.) saḥar<note placement="foot">After an improbable etymology of the Arab., from saḥar, to turn, to depart, “the departure of the night” (Lane). Magic appears also to be called sihar, as <hi type="italic">nigromantia</hi> (Mediaev. from <hi type="italic">nekromantia</hi>), the black art.</note> denotes the latter, as distinguished from (Arab.) fajr, the morning twilight (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.14.12">Isa 14:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.47.11">Isa 47:11</reference>). She speaks of herself as a Beduin who appears to herself as (Arab.) sawda, black, and calls<note placement="foot">The houri (damsel of paradise) is thus called ḥawaryyt, <hi type="italic">adj. relat</hi>. from ḥawra, from the black pupil of the eye in the centre of the white eyeball.</note> the inhabitants of the town (Arab.) ḥawaryyat (<hi type="italic">cute candidas</hi>). The <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> we have translated “yet” (“yet comely”); it connects the opposite, which exists along with the blackness. נאוה is the fem. of the adj. נאוה = נאוה = נאוי, which is also formed by means of the doubling of the third stem-letter of נאה = נאו, נאי (to bend forward, to aim; to be corresponding to the aim, conformable, becoming, beautiful), <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, like רענן, to be full of sap, green. Both comparisons run parallel to <hi type="italic">nigra et bella</hi>; she compares on the one hand the tents of Kedar, and on the other the tapestry of Solomon. אהל signifies originally, in general, the dwelling-place, as בּית the place where one spends the night; these two words interchange: ohel is the house of the nomad, and baith is the tent of him who is settled. קדר (with the <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi>, probably from (Arab.) ḳadar, to have ability, be powerful, though of after the Heb. manner, as Theodoret explains and Symm. also translates: σκοτασμός, from (Heb.) Kadar, atrum esse) is the name of a tribe of North. Arab. Ishmaelites (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.13">Gen 25:13</reference>) whom Pliny speaks of (<hi type="italic">Cedraei</hi> in his <hi type="italic">Hist. Nat.</hi> Sol 5:11), but which disappeared at the era of the rise of Islam; the Karaite Jefeth uses for it the word (Arab.) Ḳarysh, for he substitutes the powerful Arab tribe from which Muhammed sprung, and rightly remarks: “She compares the colour of her skin to the blackness of the hair tents of the Koreishites,” - even to the present day the Beduin calls his tent his “hair-house” (bêt wabar, or, according to a more modern expression, bêt sa'r, שׂער בּית); for the tents are covered with cloth made of the hair of goats, which are there mostly black-coloured or grey. On the one hand, dark-coloured as the tents of the Kedarenes, she may yet, on the other hand, compare herself to the beautiful appearance of the יריעות of Solomon. By this word we will have to think of a pleasure-tent or pavilion for the king; <hi type="italic">pavillon</hi> (softened from Lat. <hi type="italic">papilio</hi>) is a pleasure-tent spread out like the flying butterfly. This Heb. word could certainly also mean curtains for separating a chamber; but in the tabernacle and the temple the curtains separating the Most Holy from the Holy Place were not so designated, but are called פּרכת and מסך; and as with the tabernacle, so always elsewhere, יריעות (from ירע, to tremble, to move hither and thither) is the name of the cloths or tapestry which formed the sides of the tent (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.2">Isa 54:2</reference>); of the tent coverings, which were named in parall. with the tents themselves as the clothing of their framework (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.7">Hab 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.20">Jer 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.20">Jer 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.29">Jer 49:29</reference>). Such tent hangings will thus also be here meant; precious, as those described Ex 26 and 36, and as those which formed the tabernacle on Zion (2 Sam 7; ; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.1">1Ch 17:1</reference>) before the erection of the temple. Those made in Egypt<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Wetzstein’s <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> (1869), p. 698.</note> were particularly prized in ancient times.
entries.9815891bfb65314ee5a9f52ac6acaf024ce996a1: Sol 1:6 <div eID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> Shulamith now explains, to those who were looking upon her with inquisitive wonder, how it is that she is swarthy: 6a Look not on me because I am black,      Because the sun has scorched me. <div eID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> If the words were בי (תּראינה) אל־תּראוּ, then the meaning would be: look not at me, stare not at me. But אל־תּראני, with שׁ (elsewhere כּי) following, means: Regard me not that I am blackish (<hi type="italic">subnigra</hi>); the second שׁ is to be interpreted as co-ordin. with the first (that ... that), or assigning a reason, and that objectively (for). We prefer, with Böttch., the former, because in the latter case we would have had שׁהשׁמשׁ. The <hi type="italic">quinqueliterum</hi> שׁחרחרת signifies, in contradistinction to שׁחור, that which is black here and there, and thus not altogether black. This form, as descriptive of colour, is diminutive; but since it also means <hi type="italic">id quod passim est</hi>, if the accent lies on <hi type="italic">passim</hi>, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">raro</hi>, it can be also taken as increasing instead of diminishing, as in יפיפה, הפכפּך. The lxx trans. παρέβλεπσέ (Symm. παρανέβλεπσέ) με ὁ ἣλιος: the sun has looked askance on me. But why only askance? The Venet. better: κατεῖδέ με; but that is too little. The look is thought of as scorching; wherefore Aquila: συνέκαυσέ με, it has burnt me; and Theodotion: περιέφρυξέ με, it has scorched me over and ov. שׁזף signifies here not <hi type="italic">adspicere</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.9">Job 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.10">Job 41:10</reference>) so much as adurere. In this word itself (cogn. שׁדף; Arab. sadaf, whence asdaf, black; cf. דּעך and זעך, <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference>), the looking is thought of as a scorching; for the rays of the eye, when they fix upon anything, gather themselves, as it were, into a focus. Besides, as the Scriptures ascribe twinkling to the morning dawn, so it ascribes eyes to the sun (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.11">2Sa 12:11</reference>), which is itself as the eye of the heavens.<note placement="foot">According to the Indian idea, it is the eye of Varuna; the eye (also after Plato: ἡλιοειδέστατον τῶν περὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις οργάνων) is regarded as taken from the sun, and when men die returning to the sun (Muir in the <hi type="italic">Asiatic Journal</hi>, 1865, p. 294, S. 309).</note> <div eID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> The poet delicately represents Shulamith as regarding the sun as fem. Its name in Arab. and old Germ. is fem., in Heb. and Aram. for the most part mas. My lady the sun, she, as it were, says, has produced on her this swarthiness. <div eID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> She now says how it has happened that she is thus sunburnt: 6b My mother’s sons were angry with me,      Appointed me as keeper of the vineyards -      Mine own vineyard have I not kept. <div eID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> If “mother’s sons” is the parallel for “brothers” (אחי), then the expressions are of the same import, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.29">Gen 27:29</reference>; but if the two expressions stand in apposition, as Deut. 13:76, then the idea of the natural brother is sharpened; but when “mother’s sons” stands thus by itself alone, then, after <reference osisRef="Lev.18.9">Lev 18:9</reference>, it means the relationship by one of the parents alone, as “father’s wife” in the language of the O.T. and also <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.5">1Co 5:5</reference> is the designation of a step-mother. Nowhere is mention made of Shulamith’s father, but always, as here, only of her mother, Sol 3:4; Sol 8:2; Sol 6:9; and she is only named without being introduced as speaking. One is led to suppose that Shulamith’s own father was dead, and that her mother had been married again; the sons by the second marriage were they who ruled in the house of their mother. These brothers of Shulamith appear towards the end of the melodrama as rigorous guardians of their youthful sister; one will thus have to suppose that their zeal for the spotless honour of their sister and the family proceeded from an endeavour to accustom the fickle or dreaming child to useful activity, but not without step-brotherly harshness. The form נחרוּ, Ewald, §193 <hi type="italic">c</hi>, and Olsh. p. 593, derive from חרר, the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. of which is either נחר or נחר (= נחרר), Gesen. §68, An. 5; but the plur. of this נחר should, according to rule, have been נחרוּ (cf. however, נחלוּ, <hi type="italic">profanantur</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.24">Eze 7:24</reference>); and what is more decisive, this נחר from חרר everywhere else expresses a different passion from that of anger; Böttch. §1060 (2, 379). חרה is used of the burning of anger; and that נחרוּ (from נחרה = נחרה) can be another form for נחרוּ, is shown, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by the interchange of אחרוּ and אחרוּ; the form נחרוּ, like נחלוּ, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amo 6:6</reference>, resisted the bringing together of the ח and the half guttural ר. Něhěrā (here as <reference osisRef="Isa.41.11">Isa 41:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa 45:24</reference>) means, according to the original, mid. signif. of the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., to burn inwardly, ἀναφλέγεσθαι = ὀργίζεσθαι. Shulamith’s address consists intentionally of clauses with perfects placed together: she speaks with childlike artlessness, and not “like a book;” in the language of a book, וישׂמוּני would have been used instead of שׂמני. But that she uses נטרה (from נטר, R. טר = τηρεῖν; cf. Targ. <reference osisRef="Gen.37.11">Gen 37:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Luke.2.51">Luk 2:51</reference>), and not נחרה, as they were wont to say in Judea, after <reference osisRef="Prov.27.18">Pro 27:18</reference>, and after the designation of the tower for the protection of the flocks by the name of “the tower of the nōtsrīm” the watchmen, 2Ki 17:9, shows that the maid is a Galilean, whose manner of speech is Aramaizing, and if we may so say, platt-Heb. (= Low Heb.), like the Lower Saxon plattdeutsch. Of the three forms of the particip. נטרה, נוטרה, נוטרת, we here read the middle one, used subst. (Ewald, §188 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), but retaining the long ē (ground-form, nâṭir). The plur. את־הךּ does not necessarily imply that she had several vineyards to keep, it is the categ. plur. with the art. designating the genus; <hi type="italic">custodiens vineas</hi> is a keeper of a vineyard. But what kind of vineyard, or better, vine-garden, is that which she calls שׁלּי כּרמי, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">meam ipsius vineam</hi>? The personal possession is doubly expressed; shělli is related to cǎrmī as a nearer defining apposition: my vineyard, that which belongs to me (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fr. Philippi’s <hi type="italic">Status constr</hi>. pp. 112-116). Without doubt the figure refers to herself given in charge to be cared for by herself: vine-gardens she had kept, but her own vine-garden, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, her own person, she had not kept. Does she indicate thereby that, in connection with Solomon, she has lost herself, with all that she is and has? Thus in 1851 I thought; but she certainly seeks to explain why she is so sunburnt. She intends in this figurative way to say, that as the keeper of a vineyard she neither could keep nor sought to keep her own person. In this connection cǎarmī, which by no means = the colourless memet ipsam, is to be taken as the figure of the person in its external appearance, and that of its fresh-blooming attractive appearance which directly accords with כּרם, since from the stem-word כּרם (Arab.), karuma, the idea of that which is noble and distinguished is connected with this designation of the planting of vines (for כּרם, Arab. karm, cf. karmat, of a single vine-stock, denotes not so much the soil in which the vines are planted, as rather the vines themselves): her kěrěm is her (Arab.) karamat, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, her stately attractive appearance. If we must interpret this mystically then, supposing that Shulamith is the congregation of Israel moved at some future time with love to Christ, then by the step-brothers we think of the teachers, who after the death of the fathers threw around the congregation the fetters of their human ordinances, and converted fidelity to the law into a system of hireling service, in which all its beauty disappeared. Among the allegorists, Hengstenberg here presents the extreme of an interpretation opposed to what is true and fine.
entries.f3a2a9ab9aea3a52c0674ef0c3ddc4da766348ec: Sol 1:7 <div eID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> These words (Sol 1:5-6) are addressed to the ladies of the palace, who look upon her with wonder. That which now follows is addressed to her beloved: 7 O tell me, thou whom my soul loveth: where feedest thou?    Where causest thou it (thy flock) to lie down at noon?    Among the flocks of thy companions! <div eID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> The country damsel has no idea of the occupation of a king. Her simplicity goes not beyond the calling of a shepherd as of the fairest and the highest. She thinks of the shepherd of the people as the shepherd of sheep. Moreover, Scripture also describes governing as a tending of sheep; and the Messiah, of whom Solomon is a type, is specially represented as the future Good Shepherd. If now we had to conceive of Solomon as present from the beginning of the scene, then here in Sol 1:7 would Shulamith say that she would gladly be alone with him, far away from so many who are looking on her with open eyes; and, indeed, in some country place where alone she feels at home. The entreaty “O tell me” appears certainly to require (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.37.19">Gen 37:19</reference>) the presence of one to whom she addresses herself. But, on the other hand, the entreaty only asks that he should let her know where he is; she longs to know where his occupation detains him, that she may go out and seek him. Her request is thus directed toward the absent one, as is proved by Sol 1:8. The vocat., “O thou whom my soul loveth,” is connected with אתּה, which lies hid in הגּידה (“inform thou”). It is a circumlocution for “beloved” (cf. <reference osisRef="Neh.13.26">Neh 13:26</reference>), or “the dearly beloved of my soul” (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jer 12:7</reference>). The entreating request, <hi type="italic">indica quaeso mihi ubi pascis</hi>, reminds one of <reference osisRef="Gen.37.16">Gen 37:16</reference>, where, however, <hi type="italic">ubi</hi> is expressed by איפה, while here by איכה, which in this sense is hap leg For <hi type="italic">ubi</hi> = איפה, is otherwise denoted only by איכה (איכו), 2Ki 6:13, and usually איּה, North Palest., by Hosea אהי. This איכה elsewhere means <hi type="italic">quomodo</hi>, and is the key-word of the Kîna, as איך is of the <hi type="italic">Mashal</hi> (the satire); the Song uses for it, in common with the Book of Esther, איככה. In themselves כה and כה, which with אי preceding, are stamped as interrog. in a sense analogous to <hi type="italic">hic</hi>, <hi type="italic">ecce</hi>, κεῖνος, and the like; the local, temporal, polite sense rests only on a conventional <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>., Böttch. §530. She wishes to know where he feeds, viz., his flock, where he causes it (viz., his flock) to lie down at mid-day. The verb רבץ (R. רב, with the root signif. of condensation) is the proper word for the lying down of a four-footed animal: <hi type="italic">complicatis pedibus procumbere</hi> (<hi type="italic">cubare</hi>); <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of the shepherd, who causes the flock to lie down; the Arab. rab'a is the name for the encampment of shepherds. The time for encamping is the mid-day, which as the time of the double-light, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the most intense light in its ascending and descending, is called צהרים. שׁלּמה, occurring only here, signifies <hi type="italic">nam cur</hi>, but is according to the sense = <hi type="italic">ut ne</hi>, like למּה אשׁר, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.10">Dan 1:10</reference> (cf. Ezr 7:23); למּה, without <hi type="italic">Dag. forte euphone</hi>., is, with the single exception of <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>, always <hi type="italic">milra</hi>, while with the <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. it is milel, and as a rule, only when the following word begins with הע''א carries forward the tone to the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>. Shulamith wishes to know the place where her beloved feeds and rests his flock, that she might not wander about among the flocks of his companions seeking and asking for him. But what does כּעטיה mean? It is at all events the <hi type="italic">part. act. fem</hi>. of עטי which is here treated after the manner of the strong verb, the kindred form to the equally possible עטה (from 'âṭaja) and עטיּה. As for the meaning, <hi type="italic">instar errabundae</hi> (Syr., Symm., Jerome, Venet., Luther) recommends itself; but עטה must then, unless we wish directly to adopt the reading כּטעיה (Böttch.), have been transposed from טעה (תעה), which must have been assumed if עטה, in the usual sense of <hi type="italic">velare</hi> (cf. עטף), did not afford an appropriate signification. Indeed, <hi type="italic">velans</hi>, viz., <hi type="italic">sese</hi>, cannot denote one whom consciousness veils, one who is weak or fainting (Gesen. <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.), for the <hi type="italic">part. act</hi>. expresses action, not passivity. But it can denote one who covers herself (the lxx, perhaps, in this sense ὡς περιβαλλομένη), because she mourns (Rashi); or after <reference osisRef="Gen.38.14">Gen 38:14</reference> (cf. Martial, 9:32) one who muffles herself up, because by such affected apparent modesty she wishes to make herself known as a Hierodoule or harlot. The former of these significations is not appropriate; for to appear as mourning does not offend the sense of honour in a virtuous maiden, but to create the appearance of an immodest woman is to her intolerable; and if she bears in herself the image of an only beloved, she shrinks in horror from such a base appearance, not only as a debasing of herself, but also as a desecration of this sanctuary in her heart. Shulamith calls entreatingly upon him whom her soul loveth to tell her how she might be able directly to reach him, without feeling herself wounded in the consciousness of her maidenhood and of the exclusiveness of her love. It is thereby supposed that the companions of her only beloved among the shepherds might not treat that which to her is holy with a holy reserve, - a thought to which Hattendorff has given delicate expression in his exposition of the Song, 1867. If Solomon were present, it would be difficult to understand this entreating call. But he is not present, as is manifest from this, that she is not answered by him, but by the daughters of Jerusalem.
entries.ced79667ef08b4976bcceb425ecee1d64fd4308c: Sol 1:8 8 If thou knowest not, thou fairest of women,    Go after the footprints of the flock,    And feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents. היּפה, standing in the address or call, is in the voc.; the art. was indispensable, because “the beautiful one among women” = the one distinguished for beauty among them, and thus is, according to the meaning, superlative; cf. Jdg 6:15; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.16">Amo 2:16</reference>, with Jdg 5:24; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.28">Luk 1:28</reference>; Ewald, §313 <hi type="italic">c</hi>. The verb יפה refers to the fundamental idea: <hi type="italic">integrum</hi>, <hi type="italic">completum esse</hi>, for beauty consists in well-proportioned fulness and harmony of the members. That the ladies of the court are excited to speak thus may arise from this, that one often judges altogether otherwise of a man, whom one has found not beautiful, as soon as he begins to speak, and his countenance becomes intellectually animated. And did not, in Shulamith’s countenance, the strange external swarthiness borrow a brightness from the inner light which irradiated her features, as she gave so deep and pure an expression to her longing? But the instruction which her childlike, almost childish, <hi type="italic">naïvete</hi> deserved, the daughters of Jerusalem do not feel disposed to give her. ידע לא signifies, often without the obj. supplied, <hi type="italic">non sapere</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference>; Job 8:9. The לך subjoined guards against this inclusive sense, in which the phrase here would be offensive. This dat. ethicus (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Sol 2:10-11, Sol 2:13, Sol 2:17; Sol 4:6; Sol 8:14), used twice here in Sol 1:8 and generally in the Song, reflects that which is said on the will of the subject, and thereby gives to it an agreeable cordial turn, here one bearing the colour of a gentle reproof: if thou knowest not to thee, - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, if thou, in thy simplicity and retirement, knowest it not, viz., that he whom thou thinkest thou must seek for at a distance is near to thee, and that Solomon has to tend not sheep but people, - now, then, so go forth, viz., from the royal city, and remain, although chosen to royal honours, as a shepherdess beside thine own sheep and kids. One misapprehends the answer if he supposes that they in reality point out the way to Shulamith by which she might reach her object; on the contrary, they answer her ironically, and, entering into her confusion of mind, tell her that if she cannot apprehend the position of Solomon, she may just remain what she is. עקב (Arab. 'aḳib), from עקב, to be convex, arched, is the heel; to go in the heels (the reading fluctuates between the form, with and without <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi> in ק) of one = to press hard after him, to follow him immediately. That they assign to her not goats or kids of goats, but kids, גּריּת, is an involuntary fine delicate thought with which the appearance of the elegant, beautiful shepherdess inspires them. But that they name kids, not sheep, may arise from this, that the kid is a near-lying erotic emblem; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.38.17">Gen 38:17</reference>, where it has been fittingly remarked that the young he-goat was the proper courtesan-offering in the worship of Aphrodite (Movers’ <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi>, I 680). It is as if they said: If thou canst not distinguish between a king and shepherds, then indulge thy love-thoughts beside the shepherds’ tents, - remain a country maiden if thou understandest not how to value the fortune which has placed thee in Jerusalem in the royal palace.
entries.d6af5199376bdb96b5bcfc87a637ccf45322f709: Sol 1:9-11 <div eID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> Solomon, while he was absent during the first scene, is now present. It is generally acknowledged that the words which follow were spoken by him: 9 To a horse in the chariot of Pharaoh Do I compare thee, my love. 10 Beautiful are thy cheeks in the chains, Thy neck in the necklaces. 11 Golden chains will we make for thee, With points of silv. <div eID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> Till now, Shulamith was alone with the ladies of the palace in the banqueting-chamber. Solomon now comes from the banquet-hall of the men (Sol 1:12); and to Sol 2:7, to which this scene extends, we have to think of the women of the palace as still present, although not hearing what Solomon says to Shulamith. He addresses her, “my love:” she is not yet his bride. רעיה (female friend), from רעי (רעה), to guard, care for, tend, ethically: to delight in something particularly, to take pleasure in intercourse with one, is formed in the same way as נערה; the mas. is רעה (= ra'j), abbreviated רע, whence the fem. rǎ'yāh (Jdg 11:37; Chethı̂b), as well as rē'āh, also with reference to the ground-form. At once, in the first words used by Solomon, one recognises a Philip, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a man fond of horses, - an important feature in the character of the sage (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Sur. 38 of the Koran), - and that, one fond of Egyptian horses: Solomon carried on an extensive importation of horses from Egypt and other countries (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.28">2Ch 9:28</reference>); he possessed 1400 war-chariots and 12, 000 horsemen (1Ki 10:26); the number of stalls of horses for his chariots was still greater (1Ki 5:6) [4:26]. Horace (Ode iii. 11) compares a young sprightly maiden to a nimble and timid <hi type="italic">equa trima</hi>; Anacreon (60) addresses such an one: “thou Thracian filly;” and Theocritus says (Idyl xviii. 30, 31): “As towers the cypress mid the garden’s bloom, <div eID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> As in the chariot proud Thessalian steed, <div eID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> Thus graceful rose-complexioned Helen moves.” <div eID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> But how it could occur to the author of the Song to begin the praise of the beauty of a shepherdess by saying that she is like a horse in Pharaoh’s chariot, is explained only by the supposition that the poet is Solomon, who, as a keen hippologue, had an open eye for the beauty of the horse. Egyptian horses were then esteemed as afterwards the Arabian were. Moreover, the horse was not native to Egypt, but was probably first imported thither by the Hyksos: the Egyptian name of the horse, and particularly of the mare, ses-t, ses-mut, and of the chariot, markabuta, are Semitic.<note placement="foot">Eber’s <hi type="italic">Aegypten u. die B. Mose's</hi>, Bd. I pp. 221f. 226; cf. <hi type="italic">Aeg. Zeitschr</hi>. 1864, p. 26f.</note> סוּסה is here not <hi type="italic">equitatus</hi> (Jerome), as Hengst. maintains: “Susah does not denote a horse, but is used collectively;” while he adds, “Shulamith is compared to the whole Egyptian cavalry, and is therefore an ideal person.” The former statement is untrue, and the latter is absurd. Sūs means <hi type="italic">equus</hi>, and susā may, indeed, collectively denote the stud (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.19.5">Jos 19:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.31">1Ch 4:31</reference>), but obviously it first denotes the <hi type="italic">equa</hi>. But is it to be rendered, with the lxx and the Venet., “to my horse”? Certainly not; for the chariots of Pharaoh are just the chariots of Egypt, not of the king of Israel. The <hi type="italic">Chirek</hi> in which this word terminates is the <hi type="italic">Ch. compag.</hi>, which also frequently occurs where, as here and <reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Gen 49:11</reference>, the second member of the word-chain is furnished with a prep. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>). This i is an old genitival ending, which, as such, has disappeared from the language; it is almost always accented as the suff. Thus also here, where the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> shows that the accent rests on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>. The plur. רכבי, occurring only here, is the amplificative poetic, and denotes state equipage. דּמּה is the trans. of דּמה, which combines the meanings <hi type="italic">aequum</hi> and <hi type="italic">aequalem esse</hi>. Although not allegorizing, yet, that we may not overlook the judiciousness of the comparison, we must remark that Shulamith is certainly a “daughter of Israel;” a daughter of the people who increased in Egypt, and, set free from the bondage of Pharaoh, became the bride of Jahve, and were brought by the law as a covenant into a marriage relation to Him. <div eID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> The transition to Sol 1:10 is mediated by the effect of the comparison; for the head-frame of the horse’s bridle, and the poitral, were then certainly, must as now, adorned with silken tassels, fringes, and other ornaments of silver (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lane’s <hi type="italic">Modern Egypt</hi>, I 149). Jerome, absurdly, after the lxx: <hi type="italic">pulchrae sunt genae tuae sicut turturis</hi>. The name of the turtle, תּוּד, redupl. <hi type="italic">turtur</hi>, is a pure onomatopoeia, which has nothing to do with תּוּר, whence דּוּר, to go round about, or to move in a circle; and turtle-dove’s cheeks - what absurdity! Birds have no cheeks; and on the sides of its neck the turtle-dove has black and white variegated feathers, which also furnishes no comparison for the colour of the cheeks. תּורים are the round ornaments which hang down in front on both sides of the head-band, or are also inwoven in the braids of hair in the forehead; תּוּר, <hi type="italic">circumire</hi>, signifies also to form a circle or a row; in Aram. it thus denotes, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the hem of a garment and the border round the eye. In נאווּ (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) the <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> is silent, as in לאמר, אכל. חרוּזים are strings of pearls as a necklace; for the necklace (Arab. kharaz) consists of one or more, for the most part, of three rows of pearls. The verb חרז signifies, to bore through and to string together; <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in the Talm., fish which one strings on a rod or line, in order to bring them to the market. In Heb. and Aram. the secondary sense of stringing predominates, so that to string pearls is expressed by חרז, and to bore through pearls, by קדח; in Arab., the primary meaning of piercing through, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">michraz</hi>, a shoemaker’s awl. <div eID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> After Sol 1:11, one has to represent to himself Shulamith’s adorning as very simple and modest; for Solomon seeks to make her glad with the thought of a continued residence at the royal court by the promise of costly and elegant ornaments. Gold and silver were so closely connected in ancient modes of representation, that in the old Aegypt. silver was called nub het, or white gold. Gold derived its name of זהב from its splendour, after the witty Arab. word zahab, to go away, as an unstable possession; silver is called כּסף, from כּסף, <hi type="italic">scindere</hi>, <hi type="italic">abscindere</hi>, a piece of metal as broken off from the mother-stone, like the Arab. dhuḳrat, as set free from the lump by means of the pickaxe (cf. at <reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Psa 19:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Psa 84:3</reference>). The name of silver has here, not without the influence of the rhythm (Sol 8:9), the article designating the species; the Song frequently uses this, and is generally in using the art. not so sparing as poetry commonly is.<note placement="foot">The art. denoting the idea of species in the second member of the <hi type="italic">st. const</hi>. standing in the sing. without a determining reference to the first, occurs in Sol 1:13, “a bundle of (<hi type="italic">von</hi>) myrrh;” Sol 1:14, “a cluster of (<hi type="italic">von</hi>) the cyprus-flower;” Sol 4:3, “a thread of (<hi type="italic">von</hi>) scarlet,” “a piece of pomegranate;” Sol 5:13, “a bed of balm” (but otherwise, Sol 6:2), Sol 7:9, “clusters of the vine;” Sol 7:3, “a bowl of roundness” (which has this property); Sol 7:10, “wine (of the quality) of goodness;” cf. Sol 8:2, “wine the (= of the) spicing.” It also, in cases where the defined species to which the first undefined member of the <hi type="italic">st. const</hi>. belongs, stands in the pl.: Sol 2:9, Sol 2:17; Sol 8:14, “like a young one of the hinds;” Sol 4:1; Sol 6:5, “a herd of goats;” Sol 4:2, “a flock of shorn sheep;” Sol 6:6, “a flock of lambs,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, consisting of individuals of this kind. Also, when the second member states the place where a thing originates or is found, the first often remains indeterminate, as one of that which is there found, or a part of that which comes from thence: Sol 2:1, “a meadow-saffron of Sharon,” “a lily of the valleys;” Sol 3:9, “the wood of Lebanon.” The following are doubtful: Sol 4:4, “a thousand bucklers;” and Sol 7:5, “a tower of ivory;” less so Sol 7:1, “the dance of Mahanaim.” The following are examples of a different kind: <reference osisRef="Gen.16.7">Gen 16:7</reference>, “a well of water;” <reference osisRef="Deut.22.19">Deu 22:19</reference>, “a damsel of Israel;” <reference osisRef="Ps.113.9">Psa 113:9</reference>, “a mother of children;” cf. Gen 21:28.</note> עם makes prominent the points of silver as something particular, but not separate. In נישׂה, Solomon includes himself among the other inhabitants, especially the women of the palace; for the <hi type="italic">plur. majest</hi>. in the words of God of Himself (frequently in the Koran), or persons of rank of themselves (general in the vulgar Arab.), is unknown in the O.T. <div eID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> They would make for her golden globules or knobs with (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, provided with ...; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.89.14">Psa 89:14</reference>) points of silver sprinkled over them, - which was a powerful enticement for a plain country damsel.
entries.edab30ad2bdf5576cb679f730aa19eb698ea5dfe: Sol 1:12 <div eID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> Now for the first time Shulamith addresses Solomon, who is before her. It might be expected that the first word will either express the joy that she now sees him face to face, or the longing which she had hitherto cherished to see him again. The verse following accords with this expectation: 12 While the king is at his table,      My nard has yielded its fragrance. שׁ עד or אשׁר r עד, with fut. foll., usually means: <hi type="italic">usque eo</hi>, until this and that shall happen, Sol 2:7, Sol 2:17; with the perf. foll., until something happened, Sol 3:4. The idea connected with “until” may, however, be so interpreted that there comes into view not the end of the period as such, but the whole length of the period. So here in the subst. clause following, which in itself is already an expression of continuance, <hi type="italic">donec</hi> = <hi type="italic">dum</hi> (<hi type="italic">erat</hi>); so also עד alone, without <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, with the part. foll. (<reference osisRef="Job.1.18">Job 1:18</reference>), and the infin. (Jdg 3:26; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">Exo 33:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.2">Jon 4:2</reference>; cf. 2Ki 9:22); seldomer with the fin. foll., once with the perf. foll. (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.19">1Sa 14:19</reference>), once (for <reference osisRef="Job.8.21">Job 8:21</reference> is easily explained otherwise) with the fut. foll. (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.10">Psa 141:10</reference>, according to which <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen 49:10</reference> also is explained by Baur and others, but without כי עד in this sense of limited duration: “so long as,” being anywhere proved). מסבּו is the inflected מסב, which, like the post-bibl. מסבּה, signifies the circuit of the table; for סבב signifies also, after <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.11">1Sa 16:11</reference> (the lxx rightly, after the sense οὐ μὴ κατακλιθῶμεν), to seat themselves around the table, from which it is to be remarked that not till the Greek-Roman period was the Persian custom of reclining at table introduced, but in earlier times they sat (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.5">1Sa 20:5</reference>; 1Ki 13:20; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Psa 128:3</reference>). Reclining and eating are to be viewed as separate from each other, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Amo 6:4</reference>; הסב, “three and three they recline at table,” is in matter as in language <hi type="italic">mishnic</hi> (<hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 42 <hi type="italic">b</hi>; cf. <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 2:4, of the king: if he reclines at table, the <hi type="italic">Tôra</hi> must be opposite him). Thus: While (<hi type="italic">usque eo</hi>, so long as), says Shulamith, the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance. נרדּ is an Indian word: naladâ, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, yielding fragrance, Pers. nard (nârd), Old Arab. nardîn (nârdîn), is the aromatic oil of an Indian plant <hi type="italic">valeriana</hi>, called Nardostachys 'Gatâmânsi (hair-tress nard). Interpreters are wont to represent Shulamith as having a stalk of nard in her hand. Hitzig thinks of the nard with which she who is speaking has besprinkled herself, and he can do this because he regards the speaker as one of the court ladies. But that Shulamith has besprinkled herself with nard, is as little to be thought of as that she has in her hand a sprig of nard (<hi type="italic">spica nardi</hi>), or, as the ancients said, an ear of nard; she comes from a region where no nard grows, and nard-oil is for a country maiden unattainable.<note placement="foot">The nard plant grows in Northern and Eastern India; the hairy part of the stem immediately above the root yields the perfume. <hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Lassen’s <hi type="italic">Indische Alterthumskunde</hi>, I 338f., III 41f.</note> <div eID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> Horace promises Virgil a <hi type="italic">cadus</hi> (= 9 gallons) of the best wine for a small onyx-box full of nard; and Judas estimated at 300 denarii (about £8, 10s.) the genuine nard (how frequently nard was adulterated we learn from Pliny) which Mary of Bethany poured from an alabaster box on the head of Jesus, so that the whole house was filled with the odour of the ointment (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.5">Mar 14:5</reference>; Joh 12:2). There, in Bethany, the love which is willing to sacrifice all expressed itself in the nard; here, the nard is a figure of the happiness of love, and its fragrance a figure of the longing of love. It is only in the language of flowers that Shulamith makes precious perfume a figure of the love which she bears in the recess of her heart, anl which, so long as Solomon was absent, breathed itself out and, as it were, cast forth its fragrance<note placement="foot">In Arab. ntn = נתן, to give an odour, has the specific signification, to give an ill odour (<hi type="italic">mintin, foetidus</hi>), which led an Arab. interpreter to understand the expression, “my nard has yielded, etc.,” of the stupifying savour which compels Solomon to go away (<hi type="italic">Mittheilung</hi>, Goldziher's).</note> (cf. Sol 2:13; Sol 7:13) in words of longing. She has longed for the king, and has sought to draw him towards her, as she gives him to understand. He is continually in her mind.
entries.756ea15def132ae2b8f896cfa2e9a1d861a1460d: Sol 1:13-14 13 A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me,      Which lieth between by breasts. 14 A bunch of cypress-flowers is my beloved to me,      From the vine-gardens of Engedi. <div eID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> Most interpreters, ignoring the lessons of botany, explain <hi type="italic">Sol 1:13</hi> of a little bunch of myrrh; but whence could Shulamith obtain this? Myrrh, מר (מרר, to move oneself in a horizontal direction hither and thither, or gradually to advance; of a fluid, to flow over the plain),<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Schlotmann in the <hi type="italic">Stud. u. Krit</hi>. (1867), p. 217.</note> belongs, like the frankincense, to the amyrids, which are also exotics<note placement="foot">They came from Arabia and India; the better Arabian was adulterated with Indian myrrh.</note> in Palestine; and that which is aromatic in the <hi type="italic">Balsamodendron myrrha</hi> are the leaves and flowers, but the resin (<hi type="italic">Gummi myrrhae</hi>, or merely <hi type="italic">myrrha</hi>) cannot be tied in a bunch. Thus the myrrh here can be understood in no other way than as at Sol 5:5; in general צרור, according to Hitzig’s correct remark, properly denotes not what one binds up together, but what one ties up - thus <hi type="italic">sacculus</hi>, a little bag. It is not supposed that she carried such a little bag with her (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.3.20">Isa 3:20</reference>), or a box of frankincense (Luth. musk-apple); but she compares her beloved to a myrrh-repository, which day and night departs not from her bosom, and penetrates her inwardly with its heart-strengthening aroma. So constantly does she think of him, and so delightful is it for her to dare to think of him as her beloved. <div eID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12510" type="x-p"/> The 14th verse presents the same thought. כּפר is the cypress-cluster or the cypress-flowers, κύπρος (according to Fürst, from כפר = עפר, to be whitish, from the colour of the yellow-white flowers), which botanists call <hi type="italic">Lawsonia</hi>, and in the East Alḥennā; its leaves yield the orange colour with which the Moslem women stain<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., the literature of this subject in Defrémery’s notice of Dozy-Engelmann’s work in the <hi type="italic">Revue Critique</hi>, III 2 (1868), p. 408.</note> their hands and feet. אשׁכּל (from שׁכל, to interweave) denotes that which is woven, tresses, or a cluster or garland of their flowers. Here also we have not to suppose that Shulamith carried a bunch of flowers; in her imagination she places herself in the vine-gardens which Solomon had planted on the hill-terraces of Engedi lying on the west of the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.4">Ecc 2:4</reference>), and chooses a cluster of flowers of the cypress growing in that tropical climate, and says that her beloved is to her internally what such a cluster of cypress-flowers would be to her externally. To be able to call him her beloved is her ornament; and to think of him refreshes her like the most fragrant flowers.
entries.317c96d80525b4790a560651fc9c251a2b886154: Sol 1:15 <div eID="gen12510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> In this ardour of loving devotion, she must appear to the king so much the more beautiful. 15 Lo, thou art fair, my love.      Lo, thou art fair; thine eyes are doves. <div eID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12512" type="x-p"/> This is a so-called <hi type="italic">comparatio decurtata</hi>, as we say: feet like the gazelle, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to which the swiftness of the gazelle’s feet belongs (<reference osisRef="Hab.3.19">Hab 3:19</reference>); but instead of “like doves,” for the comparison mounts up to equalization, the expression is directly, “doves.” If the pupil of the eye were compared with the feathers of the dove (Hitz.), or the sprightliness of the eye with the lively motion hither and thither of the dove (Heiligst.), then the eulogium would stand out of connection with what Shulamith has just said. But it stands in reference to it if her eyes are called doves; and so the likeness to doves’ eyes is attributed to them, because purity and gentleness, longing and simplicity, express themselves therein. The dove is, like the myrtle, rose, and apple, an attribute of the goddess of love, and a figure of that which is truly womanly; wherefore ימימה (the Arab. name of a dove), <hi type="italic">Columbina</hi>, and the like names of women, <hi type="italic">columba</hi> and <hi type="italic">columbari</hi>, are words of fondness and caressing. Shulamith gives back to Solomon his eulogium, and rejoices in the prospect of spending her life in fellowship with him.
entries.808cc434f7b98c71d04166072f9356e2ebe52e79: Sol 1:16-17 16 Behold, thou art comely, my beloved; yea charming;      Yea, our couch is luxuriously green. 17 The beams of our house are cedars,      Our wainscot of cypresses. <div eID="gen12512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> If Sol 1:16 were not the echo of her heart to Solomon, but if she therewith meant some other one, then the poet should at least not have used הנּך, but הנּה. Hitzig remarks, that up to “my beloved” the words appear as those of mutual politeness - that therefore נעים (charming) is added at once to distinguish her beloved from the king, who is to her insufferable. But if a man and a woman are together, and he says הנּכך and she says הנּך, that is as certainly an interchange of address as that one and one are two and not three. He praises her beauty; but in her eyes it is rather he who is beautiful, yea charming: she rejoices beforehand in that which is assigned to her. Where else would her conjugal happiness find its home but among her own rural scenes? The city with its noisy display does not please her; and she knows, indeed, that her beloved is a king, but she thinks of him as a shepherd. Therefore she praises the fresh green of their future homestead; cedar tops will form the roof of the house in which they dwell, and cypresses its wainscot. The bed, and particularly the bridal-bower (<hi type="italic">D. M. Z</hi>. xxii. 153), - but not merely the bed in which one sleeps, but also the cushion for rest, the divan (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">Amo 6:4</reference>), - has the name ערשׂ, from ערשׂ, to cover over; cf. the “network of goats’ hair” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.19.13">1Sa 19:13</reference>) and the κωνωπεῖον of Holofernes (Judith 10:21; 13:9), (whence our <hi type="italic">kanapee</hi> = canopy), a bed covered over for protection against the κώνωπες, the gnats. רענן, whence here the fem. adj. accented on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>., is not a word of colour, but signifies to be extensible, and to extend far and wide, as <hi type="italic">lentus in lenti salices</hi>; we have no word such as this which combines in itself the ideas of softness and juicy freshness, of bending and elasticity, of looseness, and thus of overhanging ramification (as in the case of the weeping willow). The beams are called קרות, from קרה, to meet, to lay crosswise, to hold together (cf. <hi type="italic">congingere</hi> and <hi type="italic">contignare</hi>). רחיטנוּ (after another reading, רח, from רחיט, with <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> immutable, or a virtual <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>.) is North Palest. = רה = .tse (Kerı̂), for in place of רהטים, troughs (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.16">Exo 2:16</reference>), the Samarit. has רחטים (cf. <hi type="italic">sahar</hi> and <hi type="italic">sahhar</hi>, <hi type="italic">circumire</hi>, <hi type="italic">zahar</hi> and <hi type="italic">zahhar</hi>, whence the Syr. name of scarlet); here the word, if it is not defect. plur. (Heiligst.), is used as collect. sing. of the hollows or panels of a wainscoted ceiling, like φάτναι, whence the lxx φατνώματα (Symm. φατνώσεις), and like <hi type="italic">lacunae</hi>, whence <hi type="italic">lacunaria</hi>, for which Jerome has here <hi type="italic">laquearia</hi>, which equally denotes the wainscot ceiling. Abulwalîd glosses the word rightly by מרזבים, gutters (from רהט, to run); only this and οἱ διάδρομοι of the Gr. Venet. is not an architectural expression, like רהיטים, which is still found in the Talm. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Buxtorf’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>.). To suppose a transposition from חריטנו, from חרט, to turn, to carve (Ew., Heiligst., Hitz.), is accordingly not necessary. As the ת in בּרותים belongs to the North Palest. (Galilean) form of speech,<note placement="foot">Pliny, <hi type="italic">H. N</hi>. xxiv. 102, ed. Jan., notes <hi type="italic">brathy</hi> as the name of the savin-tree <hi type="italic">Juniperus sabina</hi>. Wetstein is inclined to derive the name of Beirut from ברות, as the name of the sweet pine, the tree peculiar to the Syrian landscape, and which, growing on the sandy hills, prevents the town from being filled with flying sand. The cypress is now called (Arab.) sanawbar; regarding its old names, and their signification in the figurative language of love, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Isa 41:19.</note> so also ח for ה in this word: an exchange of the gutturals was characteristic of the Galilean idiom (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Talm. citations by Frankel, <hi type="italic">Einl. in d. jerus. Talm</hi>. 1870, 7 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). Well knowing that a mere hut was not suitable for the king, Shulamith’s fancy converts one of the magnificent nature-temples of the North Palest. forest-solitudes into a house where, once together, they will live each for the other. Because it is a large house, although not large by art, she styles it by the poet. plur. bāattenu. The mystical interpretation here finds in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Isa 60:13</reference> a favourable support.  <chapter eID="Song.1"/> <div eID="gen12513" type="x-p"/>

entries.0b1f8482b2b8027e8f661470c52b96a78dc5fc28:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="1" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. I.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 THe song of songs <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The most excellent of all Songs, whether composed by profane or sacred Authors, by <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> or by any other. So this Hebrew Phrase is understood in other cases, as the <ns0:hi>holy of holies</ns0:hi> signifies the most holy; and the highest King is called <ns0:hi>King of Kings;</ns0:hi> & there are multitudes of such instances, as hath been oft observed. And so this might well be called, whether you consider the Author of it, who was a great Prince, and the wisest of all mortal Men, the two <ns0:hi>Adams</ns0:hi> only ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepted; or the Subject of it, which is not <ns0:hi>Solomon,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>a greater than</ns0:hi> Solomon, even Christ, and his Marriage with the Church, as hath been noted; or the Matter of it, which is most lofty and my<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sterious, containing in it the greatest and noblest of all the myste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries contained either in the Old or the New Testament; most pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous and pathetical, breathing forth the hottest flames of Love be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween Christ and his People, most sweet, and comfortable, and useful to all that read it with serious and christian Eves. Nor is it the worse because prophane and wanton Wits abuse it, and endea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour to fasten their absurd and filthy senses upon some passages in it. The truth is, this Book requires a sober and pious, not a lascivious and foolish Reader: for which reason some of the ancient Hebrews advised young men to forbear the reading of it, till they were Thirty years old.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mons <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Which was composed by <ns0:hi>Solomon:</ns0:hi> but whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther before his Fall, or after his Repentance, is not easie to deter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mine, nor necessary to be known.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:557" />2 Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The beginning of this Book is abrupt, and may seem disorder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly; but is very sutable to, and usual in Writings of this nature, wherein things are not related in an historical and exquisite order, but that which was first done is brought in as it were accidentally after many other passages; as we see in <ns0:hi>Homer,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Virgil,</ns0:hi> and in the Greek and Latine Comedians. These are the words of the Spouse, as all acknowledg, wherein the breatheth forth her passionate Love to the Bridegroom, whom she doth not name, but only intimate by the Pronoun Relative, <ns0:hi>him,</ns0:hi> which is here put without and for the antecedent, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 87. 1. & 114. 2. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 20. 15. Which manner of Expression she useth because it was needless to name him, as being so well known to the person, or persons, to whom she speaks, and being the only person who was continually in her thoughts and speeches. By <ns0:hi>kisses,</ns0:hi> which were the usual tokens of Love and good-will, she means nothing else but the communica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions and manifestations of his Love and favour to her, as the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing clause explains this, his Graces and comforts breathed into her from the mouth and Spirit of Christ.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 4. 10.</ns0:note> for <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thy <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>oves.</ns0:note> thy love <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">This sudden change of the person is frequent, especially in such pathetical discourses. First she speaks of him as absent, and at a distance, but speedily grows into more acquaintance with him, and by ardent desire and faith, embraceth him as present.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> better than wine <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Than the most delicious meats or drinks, or than all sensual delights, this one kind being Synecdochically put for all the rest, as it is <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 5. 6. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 13. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 9. 2. <ns0:hi>Eccl.</ns0:hi> 2. 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Because of the favour of thy good ointments <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Because of those excellent Gifts and Graces of Gods Spirit wherewith thou art replenished, and which flow from thee upon thy Members.</ns0:note>, thy name <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either 1. Thou thy self, <ns0:hi>Names</ns0:hi> being oft put for Persons, as <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 1. 15. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 3. 4. Or rather 2. Thy same or report, the very mention of thee, and all those things by which thou makest thy self known to men, thy Word, and particularly thine offers and promises of Pardon and Salvation made to sinners, and all thy works, both ordinary and miraculous, especially that great work of Redemption.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> as ointment poured forth <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Most lovely, and acceptable, and refreshing.</ns0:note>, therefore do the virgins <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Called <ns0:hi>the companions</ns0:hi> of the Bride, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45. 14. particular believers, who are called <ns0:hi>Virgins,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 2. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 14. 4. who have their senses exercised to perceive this sweetness and fulness of Christ.</ns0:note> love thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 6. 44.</ns0:note> Draw me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">By thy Grace and holy Spirit effectually enclining my Heart to come unto thee, as this Phrase implies, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 31. 3. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 11. 4. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6. 44, 45. As thou hast outwardly called and invited me, so do thou inwardly move me, who am naturally averse and backward to follow thee.</ns0:note>, we <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Both I thy Spouse, and the Virgins my Compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nions. And this change of numbers teacheth us that the Spouse in this Book is one great Body, consisting of many Members, of whom therefore he speaks somtimes in the singular, and some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times in the plural number,</ns0:note> will run after thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Will follow thee readily, and chearfully, and swiftly; which is opposed to her former sluggish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and listlesness. We will not receive thy Grace in vain, but will improve it, and cooperate with it, and stir up all our strength to serve and obey thee.</ns0:note>: the king <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Christ, my Husband and Lord, the King of his Church, as he is oft called, the King of Kings, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 45. 14, 15.</ns0:note> hath brought me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>hath caused me to come,</ns0:hi> by drawing me as I desired. He hath answered my Prayer.</ns0:note> into his chambers <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Where I may most freely and familiarly converse with him, and enjoy him. He hath taken me into intimate com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />munion with himself. These <ns0:hi>Chambers</ns0:hi> seem to note either 1. Those heavenly Mansions into which Believers are sometimes said to be brought, even in this Life, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 2. 6. because they have a live<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly Faith, and well grounded Hope, and Assurance, and some com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fortable foretasts of that blessed State. Or rather 2. Those places and conditions upon Earth, in which they enjoy the special favor and fellowship of God in Christ, as the publick Assemblies, in which Christ is in a peculiar manner present, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18. 20. where his Word and Ordinances are dispensed, and where he poureth forth his Spirit, and Blessings, and speaks great Peace, and gives forth his Loves unto his People. Yea, even the private Closets, wherein Believers enjoy much of Christ by Prayer, and Praise, and Reading, and Meditation, are such Chambers also: For it is not the Place, but the State, or Priviledge, which is here signi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied, and which is considerable.</ns0:note>: we will be glad and rejoice in thee <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>For thee,</ns0:hi> in, or for, thy Love and Favour to us, which is the principal cause of our Joy.</ns0:note>, we will remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>commemorate</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>celebrate.</ns0:hi> This shall be the matter of our Thoughts and Discourses.</ns0:note> thy love more than wine: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> they love thee uprightly.</ns0:note> the upright <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Those chaste and sincere Virgins mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. who are here opposed to hypocritical Profes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sours.</ns0:note> love thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> black <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">It might be objected, who art thou, that thou shouldst have or pretend to such a Royal Bridegroom, and such Honours and Favours? To this the Church answers, I confess, as to my self, and outward ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance in the Eyes of the World, I have not that Pomp and Beauty which Men admire, but <ns0:hi>am black,</ns0:hi> contemptible and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formed, both for my own Infirmities and Disorders, and for the scandals of some of my own Members, and for the Reproaches and Persecutions of worldly men. She alludes to the complexion of <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi>'s Daughter, who was black.</ns0:note>, but comely <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Yet I am <ns0:hi>glorious withi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                           <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Psal.</ns0:hi> 45. 13. and comely through the Beauty which my Husband hath put upon me, by his Graces and Blessings conferred upon me, such as Justification and Sanctification<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, O ye daughters of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By which she un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstands particular Believers, whose <ns0:hi>Mother</ns0:hi> Jerusalem is called, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4. 26. who had joined themselves to her, especially young Converts and weak Christians, who were startled and o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ended at the contemplation of her blackness.</ns0:note>, as the tents of Kedar <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the wild <ns0:hi>Arabians,</ns0:hi> the Posterity of <ns0:hi>Kedar,</ns0:hi> Gen. 25. 13. who dwelt in Tents, which were black and uncomely, both in themselves, and by the injuries of the weather, to which they were constantly exposed.</ns0:note>, as the curtains of Solomon <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">As the Hangings wherewith <ns0:hi>Solomons</ns0:hi> House was furnished, which none can doubt that they were most beautiful and glorious. So these two last clauses answer to the two first, and that in the same or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der in which they lie.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Look not upon me <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With wonder and disdain, because of my blackness, as it fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows.</ns0:note> because I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> black, because the sun hath looked upon me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">My blackness is not essential, and inseparable, but chief<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly caused by the scorching beams of the Sun, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> of <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ore Persecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions and Tribulations, which by Gods permission have befaln me. which are represented by the Sun, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 13. 6, 21.</ns0:note>: my mothers chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">False Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren, who pretend that the Church is their Mother, when their Actions demonstrate, that God, the Husband of the Church, is not their Father, hypocritical Professours, who are, and e<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>er were, the keenest Enemies to the true Church and People of God, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66. 5. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4. 29. false Teachers, and their followers, who by their corrupt Doctrines, and Divisions, and Contentions, which they raise, bring great mischief to the Church. See 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 26. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 2. 4.</ns0:note> were angry with me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>fought against me,</ns0:hi> as the ancients render it, and so marred my Beauty.</ns0:note>, they made me the keeper of vineyards <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of their vineyards, for to these she opposeth her own, in the next clause. Having prevailed against me, they used me like a slave, putting me upon the most disho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nourable and troublesom services, such as the keeping of the Vine<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />yards was esteemed, 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 25. 12. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 61. 5. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 20. 17.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> mine own vineyard have I not kept <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">They gave me such a full and constant employment in their drudging work about their Vineyards, that they left me no time to mind mine own, they hindred me from doing my own duty, and from minding my own concerns. And therefore it is no wonder, if in this posture and condition I be uncomely, and scorched by the Sun. But because Churches or Societies of Professors of Religion, whether good or bad, are oft called <ns0:hi>Vineyards,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 32. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 80. 8. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 5. 1, 2, 7. this and the foregoing clause may be thus understood, that they endeavoured to seduce and corrupt the Church with false Doctrines, and Superstitious, or Idolatrous Worship, and to oblige her to countenance and maintain them, and thereby disturbed and hindred her from her proper work, which was the propagation and advancement of the true Doctrine and Worship in particular Assemblies and Persons, belonging, or to be brought in, to her.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Notwithstanding all these Discouragements and Afflictions which I suffer for thy sake, and for my Love to thee. Being re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proached and persecuted by others, I flee to thee, O my only Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fuge and Joy, and I beg direction and help from thee.</ns0:note>, where thou feedest <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand <ns0:hi>thy flock,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 29. 7. & 37. 16. Seeing false Teachers and Churches bear thy Name, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 13. 21, 22. and thy true Church sometimes lies hid, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 12. 14. discover to me which is thy true Church, and which are those Assemblies and People where thou art present, and where thine Ordinances are dispensed in purity and power, and where thou dost and wiltst <ns0:hi>command the blessing, even Life for evermore,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 133. 3. that I may join my self to them. This is the request of particular Believers. For it must be minded, as that which will be useful to explain many difficulties in this Book, that the Church in this Book is som<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times considered, and speaketh, or is spoken of, as one entire Bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy, and somtimes with respect unto, and in the name of her par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular Members, and that promiscuously; and, in which of these capacities each place is to be understood, is left to the prudent and diligent Reader to gather out of the words and Context.</ns0:note>, where thou makest <ns0:hi>thy flock</ns0:hi> to rest at noon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">In the heat of the day, when the Shepherds in those hot Countries used to carry their flocks into shadowy places. Whereby he means the time of hot persecution, when it is hard to find and discover the true Church, partly because she is deformed by it, and partly because she is obscured and driven into the Wilderness, as is said, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 12. 14.</ns0:note>: for why should I be <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>as one that is <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 2 Sam. 15. 30.</ns0:note> as one <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Be really one, the particle, <ns0:hi>as,</ns0:hi> being here a note of truth, as it is in many other places. Why wiltst thou by withdrawing thy self from me, and denying thy direction to me, suffer me, or give occasion to me to be such a one.</ns0:note> that turneth a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>a wanderer,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>vagaboad,</ns0:hi> like a neglected and forlorn Creature exposed both to censure and danger, from both which it belongs to thee, my Husband, to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tect and save me.</ns0:note> by <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>about,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>towards,</ns0:hi> as this particle is else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where used.</ns0:note> the flocks of thy companions <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The assemblies of corrupt and false Teachers and Worshippers, by which I am like to be ensnared, if thou dost for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sake me. These he calls Christs <ns0:hi>Companions,</ns0:hi> partly because they profess the name of Christ, and their con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>unction with him in Gods Worship; and partly because they set themselves up in Christs stead, and usurp his Power in delivering and imposing their own Laws and Doctrines upon mens Consciences, and behave themselves like his equals or companions, not as becometh his Subjects.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:557" />8 If thou know not <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, where I feed my Sheep. For this is Christs answer to his Spouse or People.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 5. 9. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 1.</ns0:note> O thou fairest among wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Though thou art black in thine own and others Eyes, yet thou art very beautiful and amiable to me, as being washed white in my Blood, and beautified with my Gifts and Graces.</ns0:note>, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Observe and follow the paths which my Sheep have trodden before thee, of my faithful Servants, <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and others, whose Examples are propounded for our Imitation, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 4. 12. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 6. 12.
