                        </ns0:gap>. 2. & 6. 4. Joh. 14. 15.</ns0:note> O my love, to a com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pany of Horses in Pharaohs chariots <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either 1. For comeli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness; for an Horse is a very stately and beautiful Creature, and the Egyptian Horses were preferred before others, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 10. 28. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 31. 1. and <ns0:hi>Pharaohs</ns0:hi> own Charet Horses were doubtless the best of their kind. Or 2. For excellent order and usefulness, as those Horses did equally and orderly draw the Chariot, and carried <ns0:hi>Pharaoh</ns0:hi> with ease and speed whither he designed to go. Or rather 3. For strength and courage, to overcome all thine Enemies. For Horses are famous for that property, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 39. 21, &c. And the strength of the Battle was then thought to consist very much in Horses, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 21. 31. and Chariots, and especially in a company or multitude of them. And the Chureh in this Book is represented not only as fair and beautiful, but also as <ns0:hi>terrible</ns0:hi> to her enemies, <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 6. 10.                   <ns0:p n="10">10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 16. 11, 12, 13.</ns0:note> Thy cheeks are comely with rows <ns0:hi>of jewels</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Which being fastened to the Heads of Brides, used to hang down upon, and to adorn their Cheeks, according to the manner in those times. He mentions the <ns0:hi>Cheeks</ns0:hi> as the chief seat of Beau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty: and he intimates that the Churches Beauty is not natural, nor from her self, but from the jewels wherewith Christ adorns her.</ns0:note>, thy neck <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which is mentioned as another visible part and seat of Beauty, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 10. 11. But to accommodate every part and ornament named in this Book, to some particular thing in the Church, seems to have more of curiosity and Artifice than of solidity and use.</ns0:note>, with chains of gold <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by, as well as by <ns0:hi>the rows of Jewels,</ns0:hi> he may seem to design all those persons and things wherewith the Church is made beautiful in the Eyes of God, and of men, such as excellent Ministers, and Saints, righteous Laws, holy Ordinances, and the Gifts and Graces of Gods spirit, all which are given by God to the Church, and are her best ornaments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 We <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">I thy Bridegroom, with the cooperation of my Father, and of the holy Spirit. Such plural Expressions are somtimes used in Scripture concerning one God, to note the plurality of Persons in one Divine Essence, as hath been noted upon <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 1. 26. and else<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />where.</ns0:note> will make thee borders of gold, with studs of silver <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Beautiful and honourable Ornaments, such as those <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10. Variety of Expressions are used to signifie the various kinds and Improvements of the Gifts and Graces which are bestowed by Christ upon the Church. The Phrase here used may be compared with that of <ns0:hi>Apples of Gold in pictures of silver,</ns0:hi> Prov. 25. 11.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 While the king <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">My Royal Husband.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>sitteth</ns0:hi> at his table <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either 1. With the spirits of just men and blessed Angels in heavenly Glory, to which Christ was advanced after his sufferings, and from which he poureth down his Spirit upon his People. Or rather 2. With me in his Gospel and Ordinances, in which Christ entertaineth his People, and is in a special, and gracious, and glorious manner present with them, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18. 20. & 28. 20. which also is oft represented in Scripture under the notion of a Feast or Banquet, of which see <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 9. 1, 2, 3, 5. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 25. 6. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 8. 11. & 22. 12. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10. 21.</ns0:note>, my spike<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nard <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Graces of his Spirit conferred upon me, and drawn forth by his powerful presence, which is here compared to those sweet Oint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments which the Master of the Feast caused to be poured out upon the Heads of the Guests, of which see <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14. 3. <ns0:hi>Luk</ns0:hi> 7. 38. in which Ointments Spikenard was a chief ingredient, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 12. 2, 3.</ns0:note> sendeth forth the smell thereof <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which notes the exercise and manifestation of her Graces, which is a sweet smelling favour in the nostrils of her Husband, and of her Companions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 A bundle of mirrh <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>A bag of mirrhe,</ns0:hi> in which there was a considerable quanti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty of the Gum which droppeth from the Mirrhe Tree. Mirrhe is bitter to the taste, but sweet to the smell, and therefore was ever reckoned amongst the best perfumes. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 30. 23. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45 8. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 19. 39.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my beloved unto me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He is most precious and comfortable to me, and the Author of my sweet smell last mentioned.</ns0:note>; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In the place where bundles or bags of Mirrhe, or other persumes hung down, being fastened about their Necks, which yet were taken away, and laid aside by night. But the Church intimates that she will not part with Christ, neither day nor night. Or this Phrase may note the Churches intimate Union with, and hearty Affection unto Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 My beloved <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> unto me, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> a cluster of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> cypress.</ns0:note> cam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phire <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Cypress,</ns0:hi> as others render it. It was an odoriferous plant growing in Vineyards, and some think that it was a most pleasant kind of Vine, like that which bears Muscatella Grapes; yea some very learned men understand it of that Plant which dropped balm, which grew in, or near, the place here specified, as is affirmed not only by the Jews, but also by Pagan Writers, as <ns0:hi>Diodorus</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>T<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gus.</ns0:hi> Nor are we concerned to know which or what it was; it be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing confessed and evident, that it was some pleasant and grateful Plant, and that it sets forth that great delight which the Church hath in the enjoyment of Christ.</ns0:note> in the vineyards of En-gedi <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A pleasant and well watered place in the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah, Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 62. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 47. 10. where there were many pleasant Plants, whence it was called <ns0:hi>Hazazon Tamar,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20. 2.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 4. 1. & <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 12.</ns0:note> Behold, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> fair, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap> com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ion.</ns0:note> my love; behold, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> fair <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This is the Speech of Christ. The words are doubled, partly to note the certainty of the thing, notwithstanding her mean and modest opinion of her self, and partly to manifest his high esteem and fervent affection for her, and to assure her, that notwithstand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing all her infirmities, he was very well pleased with her.</ns0:note>, thou <ns0:hi>hast</ns0:hi> doves eyes <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which are 1. Comely and pleasant. 2. Modest and humble, not lofty, as the looks of some other Creatures are. 3. Mild and harmless, not fierce and fiery, not looking and watching for prey, as the Eyes of revenous Birds are. 4. Chast and faithful, looking only to their Mates: so that <ns0:hi>if any of them cast a lust<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful eye upon another, her companions are enraged against her, and quickly tear her in pieces,</ns0:hi> as some natural Historians write. And such are the Churches Eyes said to be. And by <ns0:hi>the Eyes</ns0:hi> he seems to design partly her Looks, and outward behaviour or Conversation, and partly and chiefly the inward disposition of her Mind, which is commonly discovered, and in Scripture is oft signified by the Eye, in which sense we read of <ns0:hi>an evil Eye,</ns0:hi> Prov. 23. 6. Mat. 6. 23. of <ns0:hi>a bountiful Eye,</ns0:hi> Prov. 22. 9. of <ns0:hi>a single Eye,</ns0:hi> Luk. 11. 34. of a <ns0:hi>proud</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lofty Look,</ns0:hi> all which signifie such empers of Mens Minds.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 Behold, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> fair, my beloved <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The Church here again speaks, and retorts Christs words up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on himself. If I am fair, it is only by thy Grace, and favourable ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceptation; thou, and thou only, art fair indeed, thy beauty is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quisite and perfect.</ns0:note>, yea plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sant <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">As thou art beautiful in thy self, so thou art amiable and pleasant in thy condescension to me, and converse with me, in communicating thy blessed Counsels, and Graces, and Comforts to me.</ns0:note>: also our bed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either 1. upon which we sit at meat, as the manner then was, <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 1. 5, 6. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 23. 41. Or rather 2. Up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on which we lie, our nuptial Bed: for the Union and Communion between Christ and his Church is here represented under the noti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of Marriage. And accordingly the Bed seems to denote the place or places where the Church enjoyeth sweet fellowship with Christ, by his Spirit accompanying his Ordinances, and imparting his Merits, and Graces, and Comforts to her.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> green <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Is pleasant, as that colour is to the Eye; is prepared for us, being adorned with green Garlands, or Boughs, and Herbs, as the manner seems to have been with Country Brides, such as the Spouse in this Book is represented to be. Or, as others, both ancient and later Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preters, render it, is <ns0:hi>flourishing, i. e.</ns0:hi> fruitful. So it is an happy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sage, that the Church should not be barren, but bring forth many Children to Christ; of which see <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 54. 1, &c. By these and the following words, the Church invites Christ to her Bed and House, where she may freely and fully enjoy spiritual Communion with him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:558" />17 The beams of our house <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> cedar <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not only strong and incorruptible, but also fragrant and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lightful. Though I am in my self but a mean and rustick person, yet the House to which I invite thee, and where thou and I shall dwell together, is, by thy favour, built with Cedar. Whereby is here signified the stability of Gods Church upon Earth, which is called <ns0:hi>Gods House,</ns0:hi> 1 Tim. 3. 15. and the firmness and sureness of Gods Word and Promises.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> our <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> galleries.</ns0:note> raf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The lesser Beams. Or, as it is ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred in our Margent, and by others, <ns0:hi>Galleries,</ns0:hi> wherein we may walk.</ns0:note> of firre <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, as the ancients and others render it, <ns0:hi>of Cypress,</ns0:hi> which was used in buildings, which also was strong and fragrant, and therefore suits well with Cedars.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
